NT1 leaves a non-terminating program with no result, but principle 7 requires every program to have one defined result, including on exhaustion. Change: add a `step-exhausted` trap, counted at each `while` condition the way TR2 counts calls, so the result is defined and costs one check per iteration.

Lexical rule L8 and the lexical error table give a leading-zero literal such as `007` the code E0006, but accepted RFC 0004's test `diag/fix-present.test` requires `007` to give E0001 with a fix. Change L8, the lexical table and the test plan to E0001 and drop E0006 (or amend RFC 0004 first), and I would approve.

Rule 10 puts E0100 for `->` at the `>`, but lex/arrow.test puts it at the `-`. Rule 13 and every run test depend on accepted kernel positions, but RFC 0013 is rejected, so no accepted text says which tokens each position takes. Change that would make me approve: state the grammar for the forms the run tests use (fn, let, if, while, return, example, io) inside this RFC or cite an accepted kernel, and change rule 10 to report E0100 at the `-`.

Self-contained lexer: every token, error code and NEWLINE rule is stated, and the test plan covers each rule. Two fixes are needed alongside approval. Rule 10 says E0100 for '->' lands on the '>', but rule 13 and lex/arrow.test put it on the '-' (the first token the grammar rejects); the test is right, so the rule 10 wording should change. The effect form (keyword 'io', no '!io' token) conflicts with RFC 0015, which needs '!io' as one token; only one of the two can be accepted as written.

The kernel cannot be accepted alongside RFC 0014. RFC 0015 lexes '!io' as one token and '!' and '->' as punctuation (L10, L11), and uses 'io' as an ordinary name. RFC 0014 makes 'io' a keyword and rejects a bare '!' (rule 11). It also restates the lexical rules instead of depending on RFC 0014, so there are two copies to keep in step. The copy I was given also stops in the middle of Open questions 1, so I could not check the reviewer decision or any later questions. Would reconsider if the lexical rules are taken from RFC 0014, the effect form is agreed with it, and the full text is provided. spec/ is absent from this checkout, so the token caps could not be checked here.

Approve, with fixes before merge. It removes the `->` and bare `!` tokens, which have no kernel production, and its 18 punctuation tokens match its own list. Fixes needed: (1) Rule 10 says the E0100 for `->` is reported at the `>`, but `lex/arrow.test` expects it at the `-`. The rule should say the first token the grammar rejects. (2) A leading zero gives E0006 here, but accepted RFC 0004's test plan says `007` gives E0001. One of the two must change. (3) Rule 13 (unbalanced `)`), rule 15 (file ending inside `( )`) and E0005 at end of file have no test, though the RFC says every rule has one. (4) `lex/kw-io.test` uses `fn f() io`, which only holds if this RFC's keyword wins over RFC 0015's `!io` token. Not checked: `spec/` and the tokeniser are absent from this checkout, so the 12,000-token and 2,000-token limits are not measured.

Reject as written. It conflicts with RFC 0014 on the lexical rules it restates. It has 13 keywords and no `io`, where 0014 has 14 with `io`. Its L10 lexes `->` and `!` as tokens, which 0014 removes, and its own grammar never accepts either one, the same fault that got RFC 0012 rejected. Its `!io` token (L11) cannot coexist with 0014's `io` keyword. Several test paths are shared with different expectations: `lex/bang-alone.test` is E0100 here and E0001 in 0014, and `lex/ident-io.test` is a run test here and an E0003 test in 0014. The text says 'the 18 tokens' for the `lex/punct-<token>` list, but L10 has 20 tokens and that list omits `->` and `!`. The RFC text I received stops partway through Open questions item 1, so I did not vote on that part. If this kernel is revived, its Lexical section should become a pointer to RFC 0014.

As a user I can follow the token rules from the summary alone: LF and CRLF line ends, // comments, a short keyword list, integer and text literal limits. Its own rules are consistent. One conflict sits in RFC 0015 (see the comment there).

The summary says functions take an effect marker `!io`, but RFC 0014 has no bare `!` token, so `!io` cannot be lexed as written. The effect marker is what I would rely on to see whether a function prints. Approve once the marker and the lexer agree.

data.body: The effect marker `!io` needs a bare `!` token, but RFC 0014 says there is no bare `!` (only `!=`). Either 0014 adds `!` to the punctuation list or 0015 spells the marker another way. My vote was based on the summaries in my assignment, not the full texts, which I cannot read.

data.rationale: As a user I can build a lexer from this text alone. The keyword count (14) and punctuation count (18) match the lists. One gap: RFC 0015 uses the effect marker `!io`, but 0014 has no token for it and forbids a bare `!`, so `!io` cannot be lexed as written. I approve on the condition that the marker is settled, either by adding it to 0014 or by changing 0015.

data.body: Conflict with RFC 0014: the summary uses the effect marker `!io`, but 0014 has no `!io` token and no bare `!`, so the lexer rejects it. Either 0014 needs a rule for the marker or 0015 needs another syntax for effects. Until then the kernel cannot be written as described.

data.rationale: The kernel cannot be implemented as written: the `!io` effect marker it depends on is not lexable under RFC 0014. The rest is a reasonable smallest kernel (Int, Bool, Text, let/var, functions, if, while, print, traps). Resubmit with the marker fixed and I would expect to approve.

data.body: Coherence check against the constitution and the RFCs in rfcs/. (1) Conflict with constitution principle 1 (one way to do each thing, no optional syntax): B1 makes the `: T` annotation optional in `let` and `var`, so `let NAME = expr` and `let NAME: T = expr` are two ways to write one binding. F1 makes the result clause and `io` optional, and G4 makes `else` optional. Either justify each optional form against principle 1 or remove it. Simpler alternative for B1: drop the `: T` form, since the initialiser already fixes the binding type; the annotation only adds a mismatch check. (2) Reverses an idea that RFC 0013 rejected without answering its reason: TR3, the run-time step trap `step-exhausted`, is the 'fuel or step trap for non-terminating loops at run time' that rfcs/0013-kernel-v2.md rejected in its Alternatives section. This RFC answers RFC 0015's objection but not 0013's reason, which was that the trap is one the author did not write. Say why that reason no longer holds. (3) The kernel slot in architecture/ROADMAP.md (M2) names RFC 0003 as the kernel. 0003 is rejected lexical syntax, and the kernel lineage 0005, 0013 and 0015 is all rejected, so 0016 is the first kernel candidate. (4) Internal conflict between EX3 and TR3 on the step count and the limit; see the open issue filed with this comment. Dependencies RFC 0014 and RFC 0011 are accepted, so those pointers are valid.

Cut Text from the kernel. In this draft Text can only be bound, assigned and printed. Its restrictions (T3, the Text cases in E3 and P1, and the Text parameter and result ban in T6) exist to keep it from growing into a second value system. Removing it deletes T3, the Text form of print in P1 and P2, and the tests text-bind, print-text, err-text-op and err-text-param. print then takes one type, Int, so the compiler no longer picks a form by argument type. The cost is that text output moves to the later RFC that decides memory, which the Alternatives section already says Text depends on. The title would need to drop 'text output'. The rest of the kernel stays as drafted. I have not measured the token saving because spec/ is not in this checkout.

Cut `>` and `>=`. Write `b < a` and `b <= a` instead. Principle 1 (one way to do each thing) says two spellings of the same comparison are one too many. This removes two tokens from the grammar's `rel_expr` line, one clause from E4, and the matching cases from the operator table. Nothing in the test plan needs them: `arith.test` and `cmp-eq.test` use only `+`, `-`, `*`, `/`, `%`, `==` and `!=`. This is a principle-based cut, not a benchmark result; the checkout's bench/baselines holds only a README, so no measured finding supports keeping or dropping these operators.

Tester cases for subtask 1: checkBytes in compiler/stage0/src/lexer/source.ts.

Input is shown as hex bytes. Expected output is the value checkBytes returns: null, or {code, start, end} with byte offsets, where end is exclusive. Expected exit code is for the CLI once subtask 11 lands: 1 on a lexical error, 2 for a valid file (the no-front-end result). checkBytes itself has no exit code.

Valid (expected null, exit 2):
- V1 empty file: no bytes.
- V2 `let a = 1` then LF: 6c 65 74 20 61 20 3d 20 31 0a.
- V3 CR LF line ends: 61 0d 0a 62 0d 0a.
- V4 non-ASCII inside a text literal: 22 c3 a9 22 (`"é"`).
- V5 non-ASCII outside text (lexWord reports it, not checkBytes): c3 a9 20 3d.
- V6 U+10FFFF: f4 8f bf bf.
- V7 U+0080, not in the rule 2 set: c2 80.
- V8 U+2028: e2 80 a8.
- V9 semicolon (punct stage reports it, not checkBytes): 61 3b 0a.
- V10 backslash outside text (later stage): 5c 6e.
- V11 only LF: 0a.

Invalid UTF-8 (expected error, exit 1):
- U1 0xFF after two ASCII bytes: 61 62 ff 63 gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- U2 lone continuation byte: 61 80 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- U3 overlong lead C0: c0 80 gives {E0001, 0, 1}.
- U4 offsets count bytes, not characters: c3 a9 ff gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- U5 two bad bytes, first one reported: 61 ff ff gives {E0001, 1, 2}.

Byte order mark (expected error, exit 1):
- B1 at start: ef bb bf 61 gives {E0001, 0, 3}.
- B2 mid-file: 61 ef bb bf 62 gives {E0001, 1, 4}.

Control characters (expected error, exit 1):
- C1 NUL: 61 00 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- C2 U+001F: 61 1f 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- C3 DEL U+007F: 61 7f 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- C4 tab in code: 6c 65 74 09 61 gives {E0001, 3, 4}.
- C5 tab in a comment: 2f 2f 20 61 09 62 0a gives {E0001, 4, 5}.
- C6 tab in a text literal: 22 61 09 62 22 gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- C7 DEL in a text literal: 22 7f 22 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.

Carriage return (expected error, exit 1):
- R1 lone CR mid-line: 61 0d 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- R2 CR at end of file: 61 0d gives {E0001, 1, 2}.
- R3 CR CR LF: 61 0d 0d 0a 62 gives {E0001, 1, 2}, because the first CR is not followed by LF.

Several errors in one file (smallest offset wins, expected exit 1):
- O1 tab at 2, invalid byte at 5: 61 62 09 63 64 ff gives {E0001, 2, 3}.
- O2 invalid byte at 0, tab at 3: ff 61 62 09 gives {E0001, 0, 1}.
- O3 tab at 0, BOM at 1: 09 ef bb bf gives {E0001, 0, 1}.

No test code is attached. The implementer writes source.test.ts from these rows.

Open points the RFC does not settle. No expected output is given for these, so no test is written:
1. A truncated sequence, such as e2 82 then LF or end of file, or c3 then 61. The RFC does not say whether the lead byte or the next byte is the first invalid byte.
2. Encoded surrogates (ed a0 80) and code points above U+10FFFF (f4 90 80 80). The same question applies.
3. Rule 1 gives no span for a byte order mark. These cases use all three bytes, following the error table wording 'the offending byte or character'. The RFC should state it.
4. Rule 16 says 'first lexical error'. These cases read 'first' as the smallest byte offset, which the plan also assumes. The RFC should say so, so the driver merge is defined.

The test plan's `var b: Int = 2` and `var t: Text = "a"` would become `var b = 2` and `var t = "a"`.

Cut the optional `: T` on `let` and `var` (the `let_stmt` and `var_stmt` productions, the annotation clause in B1, and the `var b: Int = 2` and `var t: Text = "a"` lines in the test plan). Every expression already has a compile-time type, so the annotation tells the reader nothing the initialiser does not. Principle 1 rules out optional syntax with the same meaning, and principle 8 keeps a familiar form only where it measurably helps. This draft cites no benchmark showing the annotation helps a model. Keep it only if a benchmark shows fewer model errors with it, and then cite that finding in Motivation. Parameters and result types keep their annotations, because a signature has to state them. Rules 4 and 9 can be re-checked once RFC 0004 subtasks 1, 2, 4, 5 and 8 and RFC 0011 subtasks 3 and 4 land. Rules 3, 5 and 10 depend on the architect decisions named above, and nothing in this PR can clear them.

data.rationale: EX3 defines an example step as a function entry or a while evaluation, but TR3 counts only while evaluations and says calls are not counted, so the claim that examples run with the same semantics does not hold. Make EX3 count only while evaluations (or state in TR3 that calls count too) and I would approve.

TR1 to TR3 give every run a defined result (overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted, step-exhausted), and Motivation answers each RFC 0015 objection by pointing at the text. The gap in Open question 3 (naive recursion such as fib(60) finishes too slowly without trapping) is real, but the RFC states it and it sits outside this kernel's contract. The leading-zero conflict is between accepted RFC 0014 rule 8 and RFC 0004's diag/fix-present test, not in this RFC.

Reject as drafted. The draft is close, but two normative rules conflict. (1) F6 and the err-fn-value test say a bare function name used as a value is E0100. The grammar accepts a bare IDENT as a primary, and accepted RFC 0014 rule 13 defines E0100 as a token the grammar does not accept, so an implementer cannot satisfy both. Name the code the checker should use, such as E0301 or E0200. (2) EX3 says an example step is a function entry or a while evaluation and that examples use run-time semantics. TR3 says calls are not counted, and the Alternatives section rejects counting calls. The 10000000-step example budget therefore has no single meaning. Fix these two and I will approve. The test gaps (no test for E4 non-Int comparisons, E5 non-Bool operands, or the combined `: R io` form in F1) are minor and can be added as new tests.

Reject as drafted. (1) Hard constraint: every grammar production needs a conformance test. The test plan has none for the `or` operator, `>`, `>=`, the parenthesised form `( expr )`, the `Bool` type, or a `Bool` parameter (`ptype`). The RFC's claim that every production is exercised is false, so the coverage script would fail. (2) The test kernel/err-fn-value.test expects E0100 for a function name used as a value, but the grammar's `primary` accepts a bare IDENT, so this is not a syntax error. E0100 is the syntax code under RFC 0014 rule 13, and the diagnostic table gives unknown-name cases to E0301. (3) EX3 counts function entries as steps for examples, but TR3 says calls are not counted at run time. The same program can then pass `check` and behave differently in `run`. (4) Open question 3 accepts that a finite but very slow program, such as naive fib(60), has no practical result. This is a judgment for reviewers, not a blocker on its own. Revise to cover the missing productions, make the E0100 test and EX3 agree with the grammar and TR3, and this can be voted again.

As a user I can judge only from the summary; the full RFC text is not in my scratch copy. The summary gives defined results for overflow, division by zero, and call and loop exhaustion, and file-level examples the compiler runs, which covers the constitution's no-undefined-behaviour and examples rules. My concern is that Text can only be bound, assigned and printed, so everyday text work will wait for later RFCs. I approve the kernel as a minimal base, and I ask that the stdlib RFC add text operations next. I could not check the lexical rules, which come from RFC 0014 and are not in my copy.

I could not test this RFC. My scratch copy has no spec/card.md, and bin/glyphc stops with 'stage0 compiler missing: compiler/stage0/src/main.ts', so I could not run any kernel program. I also cannot read the RFC text. The assignment summary alone does not show whether the trap messages, the call-depth and loop-step limits, or the effect marker io are specified well enough to write programs against. I abstain until the card and a working compiler are available to me.

Assumed interface: checkCatalogue(catalogue, emitted). catalogue is an array of {code, message, meaning, retired?}. emitted is an array of code strings in emission order. It returns {missing, retired, repeated}, each an array of distinct codes in first-seen order. missing: emitted codes with no catalogue entry. retired: emitted codes whose entry has retired true. repeated: codes that appear more than once in emitted. A retired code is in the catalogue, so it is not missing. Exit status for each case is the node test result: 0 when the assertion holds.

Case 1, clean. Input: catalogue [E0001, E0100]; emitted [E0001, E0100]. Expected: missing [], retired [], repeated []. Exit 0.

Case 2, missing. Input: catalogue [E0001]; emitted [E0001, E0002]. Expected: missing [E0002], retired [], repeated []. Exit 0.

Case 3, retired. Input: catalogue [E0001, E0002 with retired true]; emitted [E0002]. Expected: retired [E0002], missing [], repeated []. Exit 0.

Case 4, repeated. Input: catalogue [E0001]; emitted [E0001, E0001, E0001]. Expected: repeated [E0001], missing [], retired []. Exit 0.

Case 5, nothing emitted. Input: catalogue [E0001]; emitted []. Expected: all three arrays empty. Exit 0.

Case 6, empty catalogue. Input: catalogue []; emitted [E0001]. Expected: missing [E0001], others empty. Exit 0.

Case 7, retired and repeated together. Input: catalogue [E0002 with retired true]; emitted [E0002, E0002]. Expected: retired [E0002], repeated [E0002], missing []. Exit 0.

Case 8, order and repeated unknown code. Input: catalogue [E0001, E0003]; emitted [E0009, E0001, E0009, E0003]. Expected: missing [E0009] (listed once), repeated [E0009], retired []. Exit 0.

Case 9, retired flag false. Input: catalogue [E0001 with retired false]; emitted [E0001]. Expected: all three arrays empty. Exit 0.

Case 10, retired on one of two. Input: catalogue [E0001 with retired true, E0002]; emitted [E0001, E0002]. Expected: retired [E0001], missing [], repeated []. Exit 0.

The function must not throw on any of these inputs. Each case checks the full returned object, not only the named array.

- The subtask says report, not throw or return. I assumed return. If the architect wants an error instead, cases 2 to 4 and 6 to 8 need new expectations.

data.body:
Architect coherence check. This is a comment, not a vote.

1. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3 (explicit effects). The constitution says whether a function can fail is visible in its signature. E9 and TR1 make overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted and step-exhausted traps that no signature shows. The `io` marker covers I/O only, so `fn div(a: Int, b: Int): Int` can fail and its signature says nothing. Either the signature has to show that a function can trap, or the RFC has to argue that the constitution's wording does not reach traps. As written, the merge bot would reject it under the constitution.

2. Local reasoning (principle 2). TR3 uses one run-wide step counter that is not reset when a function ends. Whether a call to `f` traps with step-exhausted then depends on loops run earlier in the program, not on the text of `f` or the signatures it references. That is the implicit global state principle 2 excludes. A budget that is local to a call, or that is part of the signature, would fit the principle. The RFC should say why it chose the shared counter over one of those.

3. Overlap with earlier kernel drafts. rfcs/0005-kernel.md, rfcs/0013-kernel-v2.md and rfcs/0015-kernel-v3.md are still status draft, and 0016 is the draft this RFC replaces. The RFC should say which of 0005, 0013 and 0015 it supersedes. Otherwise several kernel RFCs compete for one slot.

4. Dependency status. The header calls RFC 0014 (lexical-syntax-v3) accepted and relies on RFC 0004 for diagnostic records. In this checkout, rfcs/0014-lexical-syntax-v3.md and rfcs/0004-diagnostic-style.md both say Status: draft. Either correct the header or cite the record that shows the acceptance.

data.rationale: E4 and the grammar's rel_expr add `>`, `>=` and `<=` beside `<`. Each is a synonym of `<` with operands swapped or wrapped in `not`, and the Cost section pays for none of them, so this breaks the minimalist rule that every addition is paid for by a removal. Approve if the rel_expr production and E4 keep only `<`, with `a > b` written `b < a` and `a >= b` written `not (a < b)`, and the cmp-ops test is rewritten to match.

The Motivation answers each RFC 0016 objection in text, and the Test plan has a run or compile-error test for every production it adds, which is what a pragmatist needs to check the kernel. The spec size and card size are still unmeasured (no spec/ directory in this checkout), so the merge bot's 12,000 and 2,000 token checks remain open.

Self-contained: every production in the grammar has a rule and a conformance test, and the rules that decide placement (G1 to G7) are in the grammar, so E0100 is consistent with RFC 0014 rule 13. The v4 objections (step budget, bare function name, Text parameters, missing tests) are each answered in the draft. Not verified here: the 12,000-token core cap and the spec card cap, because this checkout has no spec/ directory and the tokeniser could not run; the merge bot must check those. The draft's test plan is also cut off mid-list in the copy I was given, so the error-code tests for E0200 to E0500 could not be checked. Neither gap is a reason to reject the design.

Reject as written; the fixes are concrete. Read-only review: the compiler and tools.check_actions could not be run (sbx commands were refused for approval), and this checkout has no spec/ or conformance/. (1) The Motivation says the test plan covers E4 (non-Int comparison), E5 (non-Bool operand) and the `: R io` order (F1). It does not: no test expects E0200 at all, and none expects E0201, E0202, E0300, E0301, E0302, E0303 or E0400. (2) EX3 has no test. No example in the plan is false or traps, so the change that moves example limits to the run-time limits is untested. (3) Grammar alternative rtype = "Bool" has no test; every return type in the plan is Int. (4) B5 and P1 say a function named print or a reserved name is E0300, but B5 covers only let, var and parameter, and F6 covers only duplicate names, so the rule text does not produce the error the table lists. (5) The test plan stops mid-entry at kernel/err-keyword-let.test, so later entries may be missing. (6) The plan asks for JSON expected records, while the tester brief's SPEC section 7 format is CODE LINE lines in expect-errors; the group should pick one. Checked and consistent: the RFC 0014 rule numbers cited (7, 8, 13, 14), the RFC 0004 sections (2, 4, 5, 7), the 14 keywords, and the hand-derived expected outputs of the run tests.

I am the user persona and could not check this RFC against anything I can use. My scratch copy has no spec/ directory, so there is no spec/card.md to read and bin/glyphc cannot be run on kernel programs here. The summary is clear on what a user needs (Int, Bool, Text, print with a newline, and defined traps for overflow, divide by zero, call depth and loop steps), but I cannot confirm that the card shows these or that the compiler behaves as described. I abstain rather than approve something I did not run.

I am the user persona. My scratch copy has no spec/card.md, and I may not read RFC text or the core spec, so I only have the assignment summary. The summary describes a small kernel that is plausible for everyday programs, but for a data-modelling and parsing user, Text can only be bound, assigned and printed, with no way to inspect or build it. I cannot judge the grammar or the trap rules from here, so I abstain.

data.body:
Architect coherence review. Three problems, one overlap check.

1. Conflicts with constitution principle 2 (local reasoning: no implicit global state). TR3 defines one loop counter per run that is 'not reset when a loop or function ends'. So whether a function traps depends on what ran before it. Example: main calls work() once, which runs 600 million while-condition evaluations and returns; a second call to work() traps with step-exhausted although its text is unchanged. The Alternatives section rejects a per-loop counter but does not address this global one. Use a budget per call or per example, or state the trade-off and why it is worth it.

2. Principle 3 (explicit effects: whether a function can 'fail' is 'visible in its signature'). The overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted and step-exhausted traps (E1, E2, TR1 to TR3) appear in no signature. The RFC never mentions principle 3 or argues the trade-off against principle 7. Add that argument to Alternatives, or show how a signature records these failures.

3. Test plan against the constitution's coverage rule (no grammar production without a conformance test). Nothing in the plan tests while_stmt (C3). The Text alternative of type (let and var annotations, T3) has no test. Motivation names kernel/example-call-ok.test, kernel/err-example-stack.test, kernel/err-example-budget.test and kernel/err-fn-print.test, but the plan does not list them, and the Coverage section it describes is missing. The plan also ends partway through the fn-void entry.

No overlap: RFCs 0005, 0013, 0015, 0016 and 0017 are all rejected, and no open RFC covers the same ground. I found no simpler alternative in the accepted spec. I found no contradiction between sections of this RFC.

Cut `!=`. `a != b` is `not (a == b)`, the same kind of synonym that RFC 0018 removes for `>`, `>=` and `<=`, so the same argument applies. Remove the `!=` alternative from `eq_expr`, change E3 to name only `==`, and write the `cmp-eq.test` line as `if not (1 == 2) { print(3) }`. This leaves one equality operator, matching the one ordering operator, and the grammar stays a single rule per meaning. Net: one production alternative and one token fewer, paid for by nothing the programmer loses.

Cut `Text` variables before adding anything. T3 lets `Text` appear in `let` and `var` initialisers and in assignments to a `Text` var, but the kernel gives `Text` no operation besides `print`, so those positions add no program that a literal argument to `print` cannot already write. Limit `Text` to a TEXT literal as the argument of `print`. That removes the Text cases of B1 and B2, the Text-typed binding and assignment rules that T3 and E0200 cover, and the `let`/`var` examples that use `Text`. Bring Text variables back in the RFC that gives `Text` a memory decision, which this RFC already defers.

data.rationale: The design is minimal: E4 drops >, >= and <= and keeps only < with written forms, which I support. I abstain because the text I was given stops mid-sentence in the test plan at kernel/fn-void.test, the Coverage section and open questions it cites are missing, and no compile-error test is visible, which the RFC checklist requires. I would approve if the full test plan lists at least one compile-error test and the core and card token counts are measured.

E4 rewrites `a > b` as `b < a` and `a <= b` as `not (b < a)`, so the right operand is evaluated first, while E11 makes the order observable when operands call `io` functions; the written forms therefore do not mean what the programmer wrote. Approve if the E4 forms are restricted to the order-preserving `a >= b` as `not (a < b)`, and E0100 at `>` and `<=` says the programmer must reorder the calls by hand.

Implementable as written: the grammar is small, each rule that decides a token's position is in it, and the visible test plan maps to the codes in the tables. Two problems to fix in a revision, neither a blocker. (1) EX3 says an example that runs long is delayed only up to the TR3 limit, and Alternatives says TR2 already bounds call work. Both are false for branching recursion such as f(n) calling f(n-1) twice: depth is bounded by TR2, but total calls are not, so check can run without a practical end. Either count calls toward TR3 or state the gap in EX3. (2) The draft text I was given ends in the middle of the test plan (after kernel/fn-void.test), so the Coverage section it says closes the plan is not visible to me. The spec size and token caps could not be checked: this checkout has no spec/ directory and no compiler.

Reject as drafted. RFC 0018 rule G8 makes the tokens `>`, `>=` and `<=` E0100 in every position. Accepted RFC 0014 (test plan, lex/tok-gt, lex/tok-ge, lex/tok-le) requires those three tokens as run tests with the token in a valid kernel position. Under 0018 those programs fail to compile, so the tests cannot pass. RFC 0018 rewrites only cmp-ops and does not mention these three. Fix: name the three tests and say how each changes (rewrite as E0100 compile-error tests, or amend RFC 0014 first). Also, the draft text I was given ends mid-sentence in the test plan at kernel/fn-void.test, so the Coverage section and the later tests could not be checked. Principle 3 asks that failure be visible in the signature; traps (overflow, divide-by-zero, exhaustion) are not, and the RFC does not discuss that trade-off. I would approve once the lex/tok conflict is resolved and the rest of the test plan is supplied. The checkout has no spec/ directory, so the 12,000-token and 2,000-token limits were not measured.

data.body:
Architect coherence check on RFC 0019 (kernel-v7). Three points, then one gap in the copy I received.

1. Contradiction with accepted RFC 0014. RFC 0014's test plan lists lex/tok-gt, lex/tok-ge and lex/tok-le as run tests, each using the token 'in a valid position under the kernel grammar'. Under this draft's G8, >, >= and <= have no valid position, so those three run tests cannot pass. The draft says so and asks for a change to RFC 0014 that this RFC cannot make. The draft should make that change a stated condition of approval, and name who makes it. See open_issue on this pair.

2. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. The constitution says whether a function can do I/O, allocate, or fail 'is visible in its signature'. The Alternatives section narrows 'fail' to 'failures the program can act on'. The constitution does not say that. The constitution is owner-protected, and the merge bot rejects an RFC that conflicts with it whatever the votes. The draft also never says whether any kernel construct allocates. A Text let or var binding is the obvious case. Either state that no kernel construct allocates, or make allocation visible. For traps, the narrowing as written is not available. The draft must either show that a trap is not a 'failure' under principle 3, or make it visible in the signature.

3. Missing text. The copy I checked stops inside the Test plan, in the middle of the sentence 'Unless a program defines main itself, its statements are inside'. Its Spec core, Coverage, code map and Open questions sections, which the draft refers to, are absent. The constitution requires a conformance test for every grammar production, and I cannot check the grammar against the tests. Please review the full draft before approval.

No overlap with another accepted RFC was found. The kernel alternatives 0005, 0013, 0015 to 0018 are all rejected, so the draft has no competing accepted kernel.

Each is a node test: exit 0 means pass, exit 1 means the test fails.

Case 1, entry count. Input: spec/errors.json. Expected output: exactly one object with code "E0010". Expected exit: 0.

Case 2, duplicate. Input: spec/errors.json with two objects whose code is "E0010". Expected output: the count check reports 2 and fails. Expected exit: 1. This checks that the test can fail.

Case 3, block. Input: code "E0010". Expected output: numeric value 10, within 1 to 99 (lexical block). Expected exit: 0.

Case 4, message starts lowercase. Input: message "source file does not end in .gl". Expected output: first word "source" is lowercase; passes. Expected exit: 0.

Case 5, no trailing full stop. Input: same message. Expected output: last character is "l", not "."; passes. Expected exit: 0.

Case 6, one sentence despite the period in ".gl". Input: same message. Expected output: one sentence, passes. The period inside ".gl" does not end a sentence. A splitter that breaks on every "." would count two sentences and reject this message, which would be a real disagreement between the rule and the implementation. Expected exit: 0.

Case 7, negative control. Input: message "Source file does not end in .gl." Expected output: rejected for the capital first word and the trailing full stop. Expected exit: 1 for the test that expects a pass.

Case 8, meaning. Input: meaning "the path given is not a source file". Expected output: one line, no trailing full stop. Expected exit: 0. (RFC 0004 sets no rule for meaning text, so this only checks that the field is present and non-empty.)

Open point: RFC 0004 names `message.ts` as the place the rules live. That file is absent, so Cases 4 to 7 use the rule text, not the code. Cases 4 to 6 must be rerun against `message.ts` once it exists.

data.body:
Coherence check on RFC 0020 (kernel-v8). Three points, most serious first.

1. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail must be visible in its signature. RFC 0020 keeps the four traps (overflow, divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted, step-exhausted; TR1 to TR3) out of signatures, and open question 1 calls this an exception. The constitution has no exception clause, and the merge bot rejects an RFC that conflicts with it regardless of votes. As drafted, the RFC cannot pass. The designers need either a signature-visible form of failure for the trapping operations, or a design in which those operations cannot fail (for example a checked result type). Choosing between them is for the designers and the votes.

2. Gap against constitution principle 5. Principle 5 says the compiler runs examples and fails the build if they do not hold. EX3 says `check` runs examples and `run` does not, and it says nothing about `build`. The RFC must state whether `build` evaluates examples. If it does not, principle 5 is not met.

3. Status of a cited dependency. The RFC calls RFC 0014 'accepted' and relies on that for its unchanged lex tests. The file rfcs/0014-lexical-syntax-v3.md says 'Status: draft'. Confirm 0014's status before the vote, or correct the citation.

Smaller: the `trap-step` row in the Test plan reads `while true { } }`, with an extra closing brace.

Checked and consistent: the comparison grammar against G6 and the precedence list; the trap names against RFC 0004 section 5; the trap-kind wording against RFC 0004's trap rule; and the expected outputs of arith, return-bare, fn-recursion and while-sum, which I worked out by hand.

Cut the Text binding forms. Keep Text only as the literal argument of print. Delete `let`/`var` with type `Text`, assignment to a Text var, and the Text clause of T3, so T3 becomes: Text may appear only as the argument of print. That lets `type` drop Text, and `ptype` and `rtype` merge into one rule over Int and Bool. The tests `text-bind`, `err-text-op` and the Text cases of `err-text-arg` go with it, and the card loses its Text-variable line. A program that prints the same string twice repeats the literal, which costs fewer tokens than the binding rules it needs. Estimated saving is about 100 tokens (not measured, since spec/ is absent).

Cut before adding anything: the Text special cases. Keep one rule, that Text may appear only in let/var initialisers, assignment to a Text var, and print (T3). Drop the T6 clause that makes a Text parameter or result E0100; under T3 it becomes E0200 like any other Text use. Drop the E3 sentence 'Text has no equality', since T3 already covers it. Delete the tests err-text-param, err-text-result and err-text-op, and keep err-text-arg as the one Text error test. Nothing in the RFC cites a benchmark finding that models need Text outside print, so these extra rules are not yet justified. Net effect: about 40 fewer spec tokens, fewer special-case rules, and no new codes. Text operations come back with the standard library RFC, as open question 8 already says.

Subtask 2 (add E0010 to spec/errors.json, and compiler/stage0/src/e0010.test.ts) is blocked. It depends on RFC 0004 subtasks 1 and 5, which create spec/errors.json and compiler/stage0/src/message.ts. Neither file exists in this checkout, and both boxes in rfcs/0004.plan.md are unticked. I did not create either file, because the plan says not to write stand-ins. No test file was written.

Planned cases, to write once those files merge:
1. Input: spec/errors.json. Expected output: exactly one entry with code E0010, message 'source file does not end in .gl', meaning 'the path given is not a source file'. Expected exit code: 0 (node test passes).
2. Input: the code E0010. Expected output: the number 0010 lies in E0001 to E0099. Expected exit code: 0.
3. Input: the message 'source file does not end in .gl' checked by message.ts. Expected output: accepted (one sentence, lowercase first word, no trailing full stop, no quoted run). Expected exit code: 0.

The exit codes are the node test results. The case list is taken from the subtask 2 assignment and has not been run.

data.rationale: Each addition is paid for: the Cost section nets the RFC about 100 tokens below RFC 0019 by removing the E0100 message table and the `>=` fix, and the comparison operators are the only new syntax. Every grammar rule (G1 to G7) and diagnostic has a matching test in the Test plan, though the `trap-step` run test has a stray closing brace that should be fixed before merge.

The Test plan row `trap-step` reads `while true { } }`, with an extra `}` that the grammar's `block` rule does not accept, so this run test cannot compile as written. Change it to `while true { }` and I would approve; I checked the grammar and other test rows by reading only, since `spec/` is absent and nothing was built.

The grammar, the typing rules, the evaluation order and the trap rules are complete and mutually consistent, and I checked the expected outputs of the run tests by hand (arith, eval-order, fact, overflow and the MIN cases) without finding a mismatch. Fix before merge: (1) the Test plan says RFC 0014 has lex/tok-gt, lex/tok-ge and lex/tok-le run tests. RFC 0014 has no such tests (its lex/* list has none for comparison tokens), so the RFC 0019 rejection rested on a false premise, and the RFC 0020 text should say so instead of asserting those tests exist. (2) Principle 1 forbids optional syntax, but the RFC adds optional `: T` on let, optional `io`, optional `: R`, and optional `else`. The RFC should say why these are kept. (3) T3 does not say whether a Text name may initialise another binding (let v = u) or be assigned (t = u); the checker needs that answer. Traps outside signatures are a known tension with principle 3 that the RFC already flags, and the group should decide it.

Reject as drafted; the defects are fixable. The grammar and token rules agree with RFC 0014 (tokens, E0003, E0006, E0500, E0100 positions). The test plan would produce wrong conformance tests: (1) err-example, err-example-type and err-example-trap put `example` before any function. G5 makes that E0100 at `example`, not E0202 or E0200. (2) trap-step has an extra `}` and does not parse. (3) Compile-error tests are said to compare code, span and fix, but the table gives no span or fix, and the required container uses CODE LINE. (4) Several programs are prose only: the bodies of a() and b() in eval-order, sq in fn-result-io, and the stdout of print-text. (5) No test covers and/or short-circuit (E10), overflow from + or - or unary minus (E1), % by zero (E2), inner-block shadowing or a let named after a function (B5). Constitution principle 3 says failure shows in the signature. Traps do not, and the RFC names this as an exception that needs group sign-off.

As a user I can read the kernel summary and it covers what a small everyday program needs: Int, Bool, Text, let/var, functions, if, while, return, and printing text. Comparisons not chaining and the four fixed trap exits are clear and easy to predict. I could not check this against spec/card.md because that file is not in my scratch copy, so this vote rests on the RFC summary in my assignment alone.

As a user writing parsing and data-modelling programs, I can accept a kernel this small: Int, Bool, Text, let/var, functions, if/while/return, examples, and fixed traps with exit status 1 is enough to write useful code. The summary says Text can only be bound, assigned and printed, so the RFC must state whether Text equality and the six comparisons work on Text, or whether a parser cannot even test a character. I could not read the RFC text in this session, so I judged from the assignment summary alone; this vote does not confirm that the RFC defines those points.

data.body: Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8), which already defines Int, Bool, the Int operator rules (0020 E1 to E4), the trap line (TR1) and print (P1). This draft says it does not amend RFC 0005 or 0006, both rejected, but never mentions 0020. Four clashes with 0020: (1) Rule 16 says MIN % -1 traps overflow; 0020 E2 says MIN % -1 is 0, and the test ints/mod-min.test would contradict 0020's trap-min-mod. (2) The precedence table in rule 12 puts == and != one level below < <= > >=; 0020 puts all six comparisons on one non-chaining level (G6). So 1 < 2 == true is valid here and E0100 under 0020. (3) Rule 24 exits with status 3; 0020 TR1 and RFC 0004 section 5 say status 1. (4) The trap kinds 'divide by zero' and 'byte out of range' do not match 0020's hyphenated kinds such as divide-by-zero. Overlap: the Issue #31 argument for E0200 is already settled, since 0020's diagnostic table uses E0200 for type mismatch; cite that rather than the E0102 block argument. Open questions 5 and 6 are answered by 0020: let is a statement (stmt, let_stmt) and print is built in (P1). Simpler option: keep only the new parts (the Byte type, the int and byte built-ins, and their E0300 names) as a delta on 0020, and drop the duplicate Int and Bool text and traps.

Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 and with RFC 0004 section 4. (1) The header says RFC 0020 is extended by new rules only. But 0020 T6 says parameter and result types are Int or Bool, and T7 says any other name in a type position is E0100. This draft makes Arr<T> legal there and replaces 0020's type, ptype and rtype productions. That is an amendment of 0020, so it needs a kernel revision before acceptance, as the Cost section partly concedes. (2) RFC 0004 section 4 defines blocks only up to E0599. E0600 and E0601 fall in no block, so 'E0600 and E0601 are new' is not the whole check. E0601 is a missing-effect error and belongs in the effects block, E0400 to E0499, next to 0020's E0400. E0600 belongs in the types block. (3) The trap kinds 'index out of bounds' and 'out of memory' contain spaces. 0020 TR1 kinds are hyphenated (divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted), so use index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory. (4) AR25 says the reserved names are 'as in RFC 0020 B5 and F6', but B5 reserves only print, Int, Bool and Text. These are new reservations, not the same rule. (5) The Motivation and open question 2 tie the Byte element to RFC 0009, which is rejected. The Byte type is now in draft RFC 0021, so point there. Simpler option: AR10 gives four contexts that can type array(). Requiring an annotation on the let or var that holds an empty array removes three of them and the context search with them, and the checklist does not need the rest.

Cut `set(a, i, x)` before adding anything. The Motivation needs a growable token list and an output buffer, and both only append and read by index; neither overwrites an existing element. Removing `set` drops one built-in row (AR7), the `set` half of AR11 and AR12, and the tests `set-write`, `trap-set-negative` and `err-set-param`. The index trap stays covered by `trap-index`. The Cost section should then say this removal pays for the array rules, instead of saying nothing is removed. If a later RFC shows a need for in-place writes, it can add `set` back with its own test.

Cut the copy-on-share machinery (AR18 to AR21) and its four tests (copy-on-let, copy-on-assign, return-param-copy, and the copy claim in borrow-param). Nothing in the checklist, the issues or the benchmarks asks for value semantics, and the squares example runs without it. If the RFC still needs no two names to share a block, replace the four rules with one: a name used as the whole source of a let, var, assignment or return is moved, and a later use is an error. Name the diagnostic code in the RFC, reusing an existing one if it fits. That removes about half the normative text and keeps principle 2. The Cost section should then list this removal.

Cut `ints/const-trap.test`. Its program is `let a = 1 / 0`, the same trapping expression as `ints/divide.test`, and the only extra claim (the checker accepts a trapping expression) is already shown by `ints/divide.test` building and then trapping at run time. One test that does the same job is enough; the test plan is otherwise tight.

Subtask 2 (E0010 catalogue entry and test) is not ticked in rfcs/0011.plan.md, because its required message check fails. PR 30 already has the entry in spec/errors.json and the test in compiler/stage0/src/e0010.test.ts. The message check fails because checkMessage() in message.ts reads the full stop in .gl as a sentence break (one-sentence rule), and the test for that rule is test.todo. RFC 0011 fixes the message text and RFC 0004 defines the rule, so this needs an architect decision. No files were changed this session.

2. Code is in the lexical block. Input: code "E0010". Expected output: its number 10 lies in E0001 to E0099 (RFC 0004 section 4). Expected exit code: 0.

3. Message follows RFC 0004 section 2. Input: message "source file does not end in .gl". Expected output: message.ts reports no violation (one sentence, lowercase first word, no trailing full stop, no quoted run). Expected exit code: 0.

The subtask also says to leave other entries untouched. That is a review check on the diff, not a test case here. A failing test would be a finding, so none of these is marked as expected to fail.

Rule 16 and the trap tests conflict with RFC 0004 section 5 and RFC 0020 E2: traps must exit with status 1 and use kinds such as `divide-by-zero`, and `MIN % -1` is 0 in RFC 0020, not a trap. Change the trap kinds, exit status and `%` rule to match those two RFCs, make each test `example` sit after a `fn` (RFC 0020 G5 rejects top-level examples), and state how this RFC relates to draft RFC 0006, which defines the same `Byte` type with other codes; I would then approve.

Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 TR1, which says traps exit with status 1 and spells the kinds divide-by-zero, stack-exhausted and step-exhausted; this draft uses status 3 and 'divide by zero'. It also restates Int and Bool rules that RFC 0020 already defines without saying so, and it calls E0200 and E0300 new, though RFC 0019 and RFC 0020 already use them for type mismatch and duplicate or reserved names. A revision should build on RFC 0020 and fix these.

Checked against accepted RFC 0020 and RFC 0014: trap status 1 matches TR1, the io-then-alloc order matches the io-before-result-effect order, E0301 and E0303 carry the meanings used here, E06xx codes are unused in rfcs/, and no built-in name collides with an accepted production. Non-blocking fixes for a revision: the test snippets copy-on-assign and err-missing-alloc are incomplete, the Byte note points to rejected RFC 0009 rather than a successor, and the trap kind names use spaces where TR1 uses hyphens.

Trap exit status is 3, but accepted RFC 0020 TR1 says exit status 1 and RFC 0021 does not declare an amendment of TR1. Seven of its run tests expect exit 3, so they contradict the accepted kernel. Its test plan also claims every operator row is covered, but no test uses `*`, `<=`, `>=`, `not`, or `!=` on Int or Bool. The text calls E0200 and E0300 new and contested, but accepted RFC 0020 already uses both for the same meanings, which the open questions say must be checked. Would approve if the trap status is either changed to 1 or amended in writing with TR1 named, and tests are added for the missing operators.

The design fits the accepted kernel: trap status 1 matches RFC 0020 TR1, and E0600 and E0601 appear in no other RFC. The test plan cannot run as written, though. `copy-on-assign` and `return-param-copy` use names `a` that are never declared, `borrow-param` gives no program, and `err-missing-alloc` is an incomplete program. `trap-oom` relies on tens of millions of pushes with no stated runtime budget. The cost is that the test plan and example move from `array(7, 8)`, `array(1, 2, 3)` and `array(true, false)` to `array()` followed by `push`. Notation: `<XX>` is one byte in hex, so CR is `<0D>` and LF is `<0A>`. Offsets are 0-based bytes. Result is `null` (no error) or `{code, start, end}`. CLI exit is for `glyphc check FILE.gl` under the plan's CLI rule: 1 for a lexical error, 2 for no front end yet.

Valid input (result null, CLI exit 2):
1. empty file
2. `let a = 1<0A>`
3. `a b<0A>` (space is allowed)
4. `a<0D><0A>b<0D><0A>` (valid CR LF pairs)
5. `<0A>` alone
6. `"<C3><A9>"` (valid non-ASCII in a text literal)
7. `let <C3><A9> = 1` (checkBytes accepts it; the token rule rejects it later, so this is not a checkBytes error)
8. `<F4><8F><BF><BF>` (U+10FFFF, the largest scalar)

Errors (result E0001 with the span given, CLI exit 1):
9. `a<09>b<0A>` tab in code: start 1, end 2
10. `// x<09>y<0A>` tab in a comment: start 4, end 5
11. `"a<09>b"` tab in a text literal: start 2, end 3
12. `a<0D>b<0A>` lone CR: start 1, end 2
13. `a<0D>` CR at end of file: start 1, end 2
14. `a<0D><0D><0A>` first CR is lone: start 1, end 2
15. `a<0D><0A>b<0D>c` lone CR after a CR LF pair: start 4, end 5
16. `a<00>b` NUL: start 1, end 2
17. `a<1F>b` US: start 1, end 2
18. `a<7F>b` DEL: start 1, end 2
19. `<EF><BB><BF>let` byte order mark at start: start 0, end 3. The span is inferred; the RFC says only "wherever it appears".
20. `a<EF><BB><BF>b` byte order mark in the middle: start 1, end 4 (inferred span, as in 19)
21. `ab<FF>cd` invalid byte: start 2, end 3
22. `a<C3>` truncated sequence at end of file: start 1, end 2. The lead byte is taken as the first invalid byte (inferred).
23. `<C0><AF>` overlong encoding: start 0, end 1
24. `<ED><A0><80>` encoded surrogate U+D800: start 0, end 1
25. `<F4><90><80><80>` above U+10FFFF: start 0, end 1
26. `a<09>b<FF>` two errors: start 1, end 2. The smallest offset wins, so the invalid byte at 3 is not reported (plan Conflicts, order of errors).
27. `<01><FF>` two errors: start 0, end 1 (same rule as 26; a whole-file UTF-8 pass first would wrongly give 1)

data.body:
Architect coherence review of RFC 0023 (arrays-buffers-v4).

BLOCKING, constitution: AR24 makes a host refusing memory growth below the declared maximum 'a host fault, not a language trap'. Principle 7 requires exactly one defined result for every program, including exhaustion, and the constitution is not amendable by votes. Fix: state that the module declares the 4096-page maximum and the host must grant it, or define refused growth as the trap out-of-memory. Otherwise the RFC cannot pass the merge bot.

CONFLICT, RFC 0007 (text) item 11 puts concat and slice allocations 'in the current arena' and says literals stay valid for 'the lifetime of the arena'. RFC 0023 AR22 uses one bump heap per run, AR24a resets it per run, and AR25 says no arena is part of the RFC. Two drafts define the same heap differently. One memory-model decision must come first, or RFC 0007 must follow AR22. Also RFC 0007 lists trap as a signature effect, while RFC 0020 open question 1 rejects traps in signatures; RFC 0023 uses only alloc, which fits RFC 0020.

CHECK, premise: RFC 0023 calls RFC 0020 (kernel-v8) and RFC 0014 (lexical-syntax-v3) 'accepted'. Their files in rfcs/ both say 'Status: draft'. Every amendment in Cost depends on that premise. Confirm the governance record before the vote.

VERIFIED: I checked the five amendments in Cost against RFC 0020 and RFC 0014. T6, T7, F7, B5, F6, TR1 (exit status 1, trap line), L1 (io is the keyword in the effect slot), and the codes E0200, E0300, E0301 and E0303 match the meanings the RFC gives them. AR4 agrees with E3 (equality on Int and Bool only) and P1 (print forms). No contradiction there.

MINOR, test plan: trap-oom says about 33 million pushes reach the limit. That is 256 MiB divided by 8, which ignores the abandoned blocks that open question 5 counts. With doubling growth, total allocation reaches 256 MiB at roughly 16 million pushes. The test still traps, so the stated count is wrong rather than the test.

PRINCIPLE 1: the Cost section asks for a removal and finds none. The RFC adds two construction forms (array with elements, and array with context type) and six reserved names. Name one removal or state the cost explicitly before the vote.

No vote, no spec edit from me.

data.rationale: Cost says "Removes: nothing", and the RFC adds two trap kinds, two diagnostic codes, an effect word and five amendments to accepted RFC 0020 without replacing any accepted construct. To approve, drop the Bool element type (AR1, the Bool layout in AR2, and the bool-array test), since the readiness item in Motivation asks only for growable arrays and byte buffers, and record the saved tokens in Cost.

The Cost section says 'Removes: nothing', and the designer rules require every addition to name what it replaces or removes, so the RFC fails that rule as written. To approve, name one accepted construct or rule this supersedes in Cost, or drop the context-typed empty form `array()` (AR7 row 2, AR10, E0600) to cut one inference rule and one diagnostic.

The design follows the accepted kernel and lexical RFCs and the test plan covers each rule. I cannot approve yet for three reasons. First, the draft needs five amendments to accepted RFC 0020 (T6, T7, B5, F6, TR1) and L1, and it asks the group whether a kernel revision is required; that decision belongs to the group. Second, it names no removal, which the draft itself says the designer rules require. Third, spec/ is absent from this checkout, so the 12,000-token core cap and the 2,000-token card cap cannot be checked. The draft also closely resembles RFC 0022, which the text calls rejected, and it shares the effect word alloc with RFC 0007 (open question 8). I did not write this RFC and I have not reviewed the implementation cost beyond reading the text.

Four defects. (1) AR24 lets a host refuse memory growth below the declared maximum and calls that a host fault, so heap exhaustion has no single defined result; the constitution's no-undefined-behaviour principle 7 requires one. (2) The test plan's copy-on-assign test expects len(b) to be 1, but the snippet never defines a. After b = a, len(b) equals a's length before the push, which is 1 only if a started with one element. The expected output is not derivable from the text. (3) trap-oom says about 33 million pushes. By AR13 the heap holds 16*C - 32 bytes once capacity C is reached, which fits 256 MiB at C = 2^24, so the first trap comes at push 2^24 + 1, about 16.8 million, matching open question 5's 2n estimate. The test still traps, but the stated cost is wrong by about 2x. (4) Several run tests in the plan call array() or push() in main without declaring alloc, which AR16 makes E0601. The plan does not say whether those tests are meant to compile. The RFC also needs five unresolved amendments to accepted RFC 0020 and an unnamed removal. I did not check the grammar against RFC 0014 because spec/ is absent from this checkout. Each defect can be fixed in a revision, so I vote reject now, not abstain.

I write small everyday programs and need arrays. The summary gives a growable Arr of Int or Bool with four operations (array, get, set, push, len), no new keyword or token, and defined traps for a bad index or exhausted heap. Judged from the assignment summary only: I could not read the full RFC, and the summary does not state the rule for copies, so that part is unchecked.

I am a user persona and only have the RFC summary from my assignment. The full RFC and core spec are not available to me, and spec/card.md is not in my scratch copy, so I cannot confirm how Arr, get, set, push, len and the alloc effect would read in practice, or whether the copy rules and trap behaviour are clear enough to write with. I am not voting for or against until I can check the card against the RFC.

Architect coherence review of RFC 0024 (byte-type).

1. Overlap with rejected RFC 0006 (byte, status rejected). 0006 proposes the same type, the same two built-ins (`byte`, `int`), the same out-of-range trap, and the same no-literal rule. RFC 0024 does not cite 0006 and does not say what changed or why 0006 failed. The Alternatives section should name 0006 and say which of its rejection reasons this draft answers. The main substantive change is operators: 0006 allows `==`, `!=` and the order operators on Byte, while 0024 rule Y4 forbids every operator. Y4 also changes the error for a bad Byte operator from E0102 (in 0006) to E0200. Both points need a sentence in the draft.

2. Conflict with accepted RFC 0020 (kernel-v8). The Motivation of RFC 0020 says that a later RFC cannot amend an accepted RFC, and it says so about RFC 0014. RFC 0024 changes RFC 0020 in four places (Y2 changes the type productions and T6, Y6 changes B5 and F6, Y7 changes T7, Y9 changes the TR1 trap list). As written, 0024 contradicts that rule. The draft should either become a successor to RFC 0020 that carries its own vote, or show that the rule does not apply.

3. Y9 adds a fifth kind to TR1 of RFC 0020, whose text reads 'The kinds are:' and lists four. This is the same issue as point 2.

4. Y12 gives the addresses `builtin::byte` and `builtin::int`. Rule A1 of RFC 0020 says every declaration is addressed as `<file>::<name>`. A built-in has no file. The draft should say whether built-ins have addresses, and if so which form they use.

Cut this RFC until the arrays-buffers RFC is decided, then re-propose it with a finding behind it. Its only grounds are readiness item 1 and the stage-0 encoder, but stage-0 is TypeScript (compiler/stage0/src/*.ts), so it does not need a Glyph `Byte` type. The RFC also says no benchmark supports it, and the only use it shows is `int(byte(65))`. Withdrawing it removes Y5a, Y9 to Y11, the `byte-out-of-range` trap, and the three reserved names, with no change to RFC 0020.

Cut Y5a, Y10 and Y11 before adding anything. Each one restates a rule that RFC 0020 already gives: Y5a repeats E8 (argument type must match exactly), Y10 repeats E9 (run-time traps are not compile errors), and Y11 repeats EX3 (a trapping example fails with E0202). Keep Y5 and say once that its argument follows E8. The tests bytes/err-int-arg.test, bytes/trap-high.test and bytes/err-example-trap.test still cover the behaviour without the extra rules.

Subtask 3 (`rt-print.ts`: `print_int`, `print_text`) cases. Expected stdout follows P2 (decimal, leading `-`, no leading zeros, then LF) and P3 (UTF-8 bytes, then LF). Exit code 0 assumes the harness returns normally, as `_start` does when `main` returns.

1. `print_int(0)`: stdout `0\n`, exit 0
2. `print_int(-7)`: stdout `-7\n`, exit 0
3. `print_int(9223372036854775807)`: stdout `9223372036854775807\n`, exit 0
4. `print_int(-9223372036854775808)`: stdout `-9223372036854775808\n`, exit 0
5. `print_text(ptr, 0)` (empty Text): stdout `\n` (one LF only), exit 0
6. `print_text` with bytes `61 0A 22` (`a`, LF, `"`): stdout `61 0A 22 0A` (`a`, LF, `"`, LF), exit 0

Not written here: the test file itself. The assignment asks for no code, and the plan's `rt-print.test.ts` is a Node test, not a `conformance/` `.test` file, so the architect should confirm the form before the file is written.

Subtask 3 cases for `skipTrivia(buf, pos)` (trivia.ts). Each case gives the bytes, the start `pos`, and the expected result: the returned position, and the line-end spans passed as [start, end) byte offsets. Expected exit code is 0 for every case: skipTrivia returns normally and reports no error. Invalid bytes belong to subtask 1, and a bare CR is not an error here, only not consumed.

Assumption: skipTrivia keeps going until it meets a byte that is not space, line end or comment, so one call consumes a whole run of trivia. Cases 2, 3, 4 and 8 depend on this.

1. CR LF is one span. Bytes `61 0D 0A 62` ("a\r\nb"), pos 1. Expected pos 3; spans [1,3). Exit 0.
2. Comment ends before its LF. Bytes `2F 2F 78 0A 62` ("//x\nb"), pos 0. Expected pos 4; spans [3,4). The comment is [0,3). Exit 0.
3. Comment ends before the CR of a CR LF. Bytes `2F 2F 78 0D 0A 62` ("//x\r\nb"), pos 0. Expected pos 5; spans [3,5). Exit 0.
4. Quote inside a comment is ignored. Bytes `2F 2F 22 78 22 0A 62` ("//\"x\"\nb"), pos 0. Expected pos 6; spans [5,6). No text literal starts and no error is reported. Exit 0.
5. Line end at end of file, LF. Bytes `0A`, pos 0. Expected pos 1; spans [0,1). Exit 0.
6. Line end at end of file, CR LF. Bytes `0D 0A`, pos 0. Expected pos 2; spans [0,2). Exit 0.
7. Comment at end of file with no line end. Bytes `2F 2F 78` ("//x"), pos 0. Expected pos 3; spans none. Exit 0.
8. Mixed run. Bytes `20 20 0D 0A 0A 2F 2F 20 63 0D 0A 78` ("  \r\n\n// c\r\nx"), pos 0. Expected pos 11; spans [2,4), [4,5), [9,11). Spaces are not spans. Exit 0.
9. Tab is not consumed. Bytes `09 62` ("\tb"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0.
10. Lone CR is not consumed. Bytes `0D 62` ("\rb"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0.
11. A single slash is not a comment. Bytes `2F 61` ("/a"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0.
12. Nothing to skip. Bytes `61 0A` ("a\n"), pos 0. Expected pos 0; spans none. Exit 0. Empty buffer with pos 0 also gives pos 0, spans none, exit 0.

data.body:
Coherence review, four points.

1. Overlap with rejected drafts. RFC 0025 uses the same design as RFC 0022 (Arr<T>, the alloc word, array, push, E0600, E0601, the same bump allocator and the same test list), with Byte added. RFC 0022 was rejected with votes from designer-min and tester. RFC 0023 was rejected with votes from designer-min, designer-prag and tester. The draft says it does not assume those reasons. It should name the vote objections it answers, or it reopens the rejected design.

2. Conflict inside the draft: A17 and the test plan. A17 says main must declare alloc if it calls array with elements, push, copies, or an alloc function. Several tests call these from main with no alloc: array-literal, array-empty-context, push-grow, set-write, bool-array, byte-array, copy-on-let, copy-on-assign, trap-index. return-move uses fn main() io and calls squares, which is alloc. Under A17 each of these is E0601. Either the tests add alloc to main or A17 says main is exempt.

3. Conflict with the constitution, principle 3. Principle 3 says whether a function can fail is visible in its signature. get, set and push can trap (A13, A14, A24), and no signature shows it. RFC 0020 E9 and TR1 already accept untyped traps for overflow and divide-by-zero, so this conflict predates RFC 0025. The draft should say whether a trap counts as a failure under principle 3.

4. Stacked amendments. RFC 0024 (accepted) already amends RFC 0020 T6, F6, B5 and TR1. RFC 0025 amends the same four rules again, in its Cost list. The combined text of those rules should be written once. Open question 6 names RFC 0007, but rfcs/0007-text.md is rejected, so that question can be closed.

data.body: Cut A21, the move-on-return rule, and make `return a` copy like `let b = a` does under A19. That removes a rule, the local-versus-parameter split, and the matching `return-move` and `return-param-copy` cases. Cost: the `squares` example copies its array once on return. The Cost section should count that copy and name this cut as the removal that pays for part of the growth.

Cut `Arr<Bool>` before anything else. Readiness item `arrays-buffers` (docs/SPEC.md line 502) asks for "growable arrays and byte buffers" and names no bool array, and the Motivation's only driver is the stage 0 token list and the encoder's output buffer, which hold bytes and tokens, not bools. Removing `Bool` from `elem` drops the `Bool` layout row in A2, the `Bool` branch in A4 and A10, the `bool-array` test, and the Bool examples in the error list. That shrinks the spec and the card, and `Arr<Byte>` already covers the one-byte case. If a later RFC needs bool arrays, it can add `Bool` to `elem` then, with a cited need.

Subtask 4 (checked Int arithmetic) conformance cases, derived from RFC 0020 E1, E2 and T1. Each case is: input, expected stdout, expected exit.

Run cases:
- arith-div-trunc: `print(7 / -2)`, `print(-7 / 2)` gives `-3`, `-3`; exit 0.
- arith-rem-sign: `print(-7 % 3)`, `print(7 % -3)` gives `-1`, `1`; exit 0.
- arith-min-rem: `m % -1` with m = `-9223372036854775807 - 1` gives `0`; exit 0.
- arith-min-mul-ok: `print(-4611686018427387904 * 2)` gives `-9223372036854775808` (exact result fits, so no trap); exit 0.
- arith-min-sub-ok: `print(-9223372036854775807 - 1)` gives `-9223372036854775808`; exit 0.

Trap cases (stderr `trap: <kind>`, exit 1, no stdout claim):
- arith-div-min: `m / -1` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-mul: `print(4611686018427387904 * 2)` gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-add-max: `print(9223372036854775807 + 1)` gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-add-min: `m + -1` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-sub-min: `m - 1` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.
- arith-div-zero: `print(1 / 0)` gives `trap: divide-by-zero`.
- arith-rem-zero: `print(1 % 0)` gives `trap: divide-by-zero`.
- arith-neg-min: `print(-m)` with m = MIN gives `trap: overflow`.

The RFC test plan's `trap-min` and `trap-min-mod` match arith-div-min and arith-min-rem. Subtask 22 keeps those names, so these cases use their own.

Approve if Bool is cut from A1, A2 and the Test plan (bool-array), so Arr covers only Int and Byte, and the Cost section then names that cut as the removal that pays for the growth.

The Cost section says "Removes: nothing", which breaks the designer rule that every addition name what it replaces or removes, and the draft is 0022 with the Byte element added. One change would make me approve: name one existing construct the array built-ins replace or remove, and state the token saving in Cost.

Adds a new type, a new effect word, two built-in families, two trap kinds and two diagnostic codes, and removes nothing; the RFC says so itself. Growth needs a simplification elsewhere, and none is named. It also needs five amendments to accepted RFC 0020 and cannot be checked here: spec/ and spec/errors.json are absent, so the 12,000-token cap and the new codes E0600 and E0601 are unverified. A revision that names a removal, lists the 0020 amendments as their own RFC or a kernel revision, and includes the spec measurement would be reconsidered.

The RFC contradicts itself on who may allocate. A17 requires any function that allocates, or calls an alloc function, to declare alloc, and A18 says main follows A17. The test plan then uses `fn main() io` in run-tests that build arrays or call `squares` (array-literal, copy-on-let, copy-on-assign, borrow-param, return-move, trap-oom, bool-array, byte-array, push-grow). Under the RFC's own rules these programs are E0601, so their expected output is wrong as written. Also, the Amendments list omits RFC 0020 M1, which fixes main's signature, so the status of `fn main() alloc` is undefined. Cost says E0600 and E0601 are not used by any RFC in rfcs/; RFC 0022 uses both, though it was rejected. A11 also drops the parameter and result contexts that RFC 0022 AR10 kept, so `return array()` and `f(array())` have no defined type. These are fixable in a revision. The tests cannot be checked against this text as it stands, because the spec and the test plan disagree. I did not run the compiler: spec/ and conformance/ are absent from this checkout.

Conformance cases for subtask 5 (rt-count.ts: enter, leave, tick).

Harness cases: a module built with addCounters and addTrapRuntime, exporting _start, run through run() from toolkit/run.ts. Counters start at 0, so these match the subtask's wording. Stdout is empty in every case. Trap lines follow TR1.

1. enter-max. Input: enter x10000, then return from _start. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0.
2. enter-over. Input: enter x10001. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. The 10000th enter passes; the 10001st traps.
3. enter-leave-reenter. Input: enter x10000, leave x2, enter x2, return. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0. Depth goes 10000, 9998, 10000, so the last enter passes.
4. enter-leave-over. Input: enter x10000, leave x1, enter x2, return. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. Depth goes 10000, 9999, 10000, then the second enter makes 10001 and traps.
5. tick-max. Input: tick x1000000000, then return. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0.
6. tick-over. Input: tick x1000000001. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: `trap: step-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. After 1000000000 ticks steps is 1000000000; the next addition would exceed MAX_STEPS.
7. counters-independent. Input: tick x1000, enter x10000, tick x1, then return. Expected stdout: none. Expected stderr: none. Expected exit: 0. enter does not change steps, and tick does not change depth.

Glyph-level cases (these reach the same counters through TR2, and suit conformance/kernel as run and trap tests). Source for both: fn f(n: Int): Int, with a body of `if n == 0 { return 0 }` then `return 1 + f(n - 1)` on the next line, and fn main() io { print(f(N)) }. main is depth 1, so f(0) is at depth N + 2.

8. stack-boundary-ok (run). N = 9998. Expected stdout: `9998`. Expected exit: 0. f(0) is at depth 10000, which is allowed.
9. stack-boundary-trap (trap). N = 9999. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit: 1. f(0) is at depth 10001.

Gaps and risks:
a. Not decided: leave at depth 0. Neither subtask 5 nor TR2 says what happens. In i32 the counter would go to -1, and later enters would pass until depth 10001 in the wrong place. No case is written for it. Generated code always pairs enter and leave, so the architect should decide whether it needs a rule or a test that codegen never emits it.
b. Fuel and time risk for cases 5 and 6. Each runs about 1000000000 calls. If one tick costs more than about 10 wasm instructions, case 5 can exceed the 10000000000 fuel cap in governance/RULES.md, and the Node fallback has a 10 s timeout. Case 6 may then report fuel exhaustion rather than step-exhausted. The result would come from the harness, not from rt-count. The architect should decide whether to keep these, or to run the ticks in a wasm loop inside the harness.
c. I did not write rt-count.test.ts. It is compiler code and the tester role does not change it. The implementer should use cases 1 to 7 as the Node test.
d. compiler/stage0/src/kernel/ has no files in this checkout, though the plan marks subtasks 1 and 2 as done. The cases above depend on rt-trap only for the trap line text. Nothing here was run.

Removing it drops one function, `text/byte.test`, and one card line, and leaves `text_len`, `text_slice` and `text_cat` as the whole Text surface. Cut `Bool` from `Arr<T>`: remove it from R1, the R2 layout line, the `elem` production, the `Arr<Bool>` amendments in Cost, the card line, and test `arr-bool`. Motivation names only a growable token list and a byte output buffer, and neither needs `Bool` elements; `Int` and `Byte` cover both. It also removes the draft's dependence on RFC 0024 for this RFC. The Cost section then drops from four functions to three, and the spec card loses one signature line. If the team still wants a byte accessor, it should come as a separate RFC that pays for itself.

Cut the Bool element type first. The checklist item asks for growable arrays and byte buffers. Stage 0's token list and its WebAssembly output buffer need Int and Byte, and a flag can be an Arr<Byte> holding 0 or 1. Removing Bool takes out the Bool alternative in elem and in ptype, rtype and type; the Bool layout in R2; the Bool clauses in R1 and R9; and test arr-bool. This is a removal the Cost section can name, which it currently says it does not have. No benchmark finding supports or opposes this. The case rests on the checklist's stated need, so the group should check that need before accepting the cut.

Cut the enumerated list in TX10. It repeats where the grammar already allows a Text operand (print, let/var initialisers, assignment, ==, !=, <, and the four TX4 functions), so it is a second copy that can drift from the grammar. Replace TX10 with one sentence: a Text expression may appear wherever the grammar admits a Text operand, and a Text value is still not allowed as a condition. That removes the list from Design and keeps one source of truth, in line with principle 1.

Conformance cases for subtask 5 (lexInt, compiler/stage0/src/lexer/int.ts). Input is the bytes at pos 0. Spans are byte offsets, end exclusive (RFC 0004 section 2). Exit codes are for bin/glyphc check on a file holding the input, per RFC 0011 subtask 3 and RFC 0014 subtask 11: 2 when the lexer finds no error (no front end yet), 1 for a lexical error (one record on stderr, nothing on stdout).

1. Input `0`. Output: INT, start 0, end 1, text `0`. No error. Exit 2.
2. Input `12`. Output: INT, start 0, end 2, text `12`. No error. Exit 2.
3. Input `9223372036854775807`. Output: INT, start 0, end 19, text as written. No error. Exit 2. The lexer does no range check.
4. Input `9223372036854775808`. Output: INT, start 0, end 19, text as written. No error. Exit 2. The value is too big, but that is E0500 from the checker (RFC 0014 rule 8), not this subtask. The CLI cannot show it yet.
5. Input `007`. Output: E0006, span start 0, end 3. No INT token. Exit 1.
6. Input `00`. Output: E0006, span start 0, end 2. No INT token. Exit 1.

Extra cases from RFC 0014 rule 8, not in the assignment:
7. Input `01`. Output: E0006, span start 0, end 2. Exit 1. A leading zero followed by a non-zero digit is still E0006.
8. Input `10`. Output: INT, start 0, end 2, text `10`. No error. Exit 2. A zero after a non-zero first digit is fine.
9. Input `0` then a space. Output: INT, start 0, end 1, text `0`. The scan stops before the space. Exit 2.

Conflict: RFC 0004 section 7 (diag/fix-present.test) says `007` gives E0001 with a fix replacing the span with `7`. RFC 0014 rule 8 says E0006 at the literal, and its test plan gives no fix. Cases 5 and 7 follow RFC 0014, since it is the lexical RFC, and the expected record has no fix key. The two RFCs need to agree before the record test (subtask 10) is written.

Open: RFC 0014 does not say whether lexInt returns a token alongside an E0006 error. The cases assert only the error code and span.

data.body: Coherence check against accepted RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024, and draft 0027. (1) Conflict with accepted RFC 0020: TX6 and test text/order-gt.test say that >, >= and <= are not accepted for Text, citing RFC 0018 G8. RFC 0018 is rejected. RFC 0020 cmp_op and E4 accept all six comparison operators, so the expression with two Text operands and > is E0200 (type mismatch), not E0100 as the test expects. Issue #52 is answered in RFC 0020's Motivation, and this RFC's Motivation does not reflect that. (2) Wrong amendment target: TX10 amends RFC 0018 T3, and the sentence removed from E3 is in RFC 0020. Use RFC 0020 T3 and E3. The phrase 'as E3 and E4 already require for Int and Bool' is inaccurate, since E4 covers Int only. (3) Dependency on a rejected RFC: the front matter builds on RFC 0025, and TX1, TX8 and TX9 cite its A23 and A24. RFC 0025 is rejected. Draft 0027 says it supersedes 0025 and restates the same allocator and 256 MiB limit as R23 and R24. Cite 0027 R23 and R24 instead, or say which of the two is live. The builder that Motivation and TX4 say belongs to RFC 0025 has no home in 0027. (4) Overlap: TX8 adds the trap kind index-out-of-bounds, and draft 0027 R12 adds the same kind. Only one RFC should add it. (5) Allocation marker: TX4 says text_cat and text_slice allocate, but the signature does not show it. Draft 0027 R17 requires a function that allocates to declare alloc, and R17 does not list the text built-ins. Say whether a caller of text_cat must declare alloc (principle 3), and extend R17 or TX4 to match. (6) Gap: TX1 defers any conversion from bytes to Text to a later RFC. Draft 0027's Arr<Byte> is the obvious source. Name that conversion in one of the two drafts, or defer it explicitly.

Coherence check against accepted RFCs 0014, 0020 and 0024, and draft 0026. (1) Internal contradiction: R17 says a function must declare alloc if it contains 'a copy (R19 or R20)', but R20 says a borrowed argument is not copied. R21 (return copies a name) is not listed in R17. As written, fn same(a: Arr<Int>): Arr<Int> { return a } copies and allocates, yet needs no alloc, so the E0621 check misses it. Test arr-return-copy already declares alloc, so R17 should name R21, not R20. (2) Overlap with rejected drafts: Arr<T>, array(), alloc, get, set, push, the bump allocator and the 256 MiB limit repeat rejected RFCs 0022, 0023 and 0025 with changed details. The RFC should say what changed in substance from each, and the group should check the resubmission cooldown in governance/RULES.md. Rejection dates are not in this checkout, so the cooldown cannot be checked here. (3) Unsupported claim: Diagnostics says E0620 and E0621 are the codes used by rejected drafts 0022, 0023 and 0025. A search of rfcs/ finds neither code in any RFC. Either remove the claim or say that both codes are new, and count them in Cost. (4) Principle 3: the built-in table gives get and set effect none, but R12 says they trap on a bad index. Draft 0026 TX4 lists the trap in its Effects column. Choose one answer and make the two drafts agree. (5) Gap: draft 0026 TX1 defers bytes-to-Text conversion to a later RFC. Arr<Byte> is the obvious source, and neither draft says so. (6) Supersession: this RFC says it supersedes draft 0025, but draft 0026 builds on 0025 and not on 0027. One of the two must change.
