data.rationale: The four functions in TX4 (text_len, text_byte, text_slice, text_cat) with the TX6 comparison are the smallest set that covers the checklist's indexing, slicing, comparison and building, and the Cost section removes the T3 and E3 sentences that block them; I checked both against accepted RFC 0020 (T3 and E3). Cost is about 260 tokens, unmeasured because spec/ is absent.

Cost says it removes nothing and adds two trap kinds, two error codes, a new effect word and five amendments to accepted RFC 0020, which breaks the rule that every addition is paid for by a removal. To approve, name one accepted construct it removes, for example drop Arr<Bool> and Arr<Byte> for the first milestone, since Bool can be stored as Int 0 or 1 and that removes the elem production, the R2 layout for two types and the duplicated copy rules.

The draft is complete: grammar, rules R1 to R25, a test plan with run and compile-error tests, and answers to issues #31, #32 and #36. It cites no benchmark finding, and its Cost section is unmeasured because spec/ is absent, so I cannot yet check the 12,000-token cap or whether the surface helps models. I would approve once a measured cost is attached, or once a finding shows models get array indexing and implicit copies right.

TX4 lists traps and allocation only in a table, but the signatures (`(Text, Int) -> Byte`, `(Text, Text) -> Text`) do not show them. Constitution principle 3 requires that whether a function can allocate or fail is visible in its signature, and Open Question 2 admits the gap. Would approve if the signatures of text_byte, text_slice and text_cat carry the trap and allocation effects in the declaration syntax, that syntax is defined in this RFC, and RFC 0025's get and set use the same marker.

The memory rules point at RFC 0025, which RFC 0027 lists as rejected. TX1, TX8 and TX9 cite RFC 0025 A23 and A24 for the heap limit, the bump allocator and out-of-memory, and TX11 waits on the RFC 0025 memory decision. The draft also says text_cat and text_slice allocate, but it does not say they need the alloc effect word. Under principle 3 a function that calls them should show that in its signature. Reject now; resubmit with the allocator rules stated in this RFC or in one accepted RFC, and with the alloc rule named.

The base rules say growth needs a simplification elsewhere. The Cost section adds about 550 tokens and names no removal from the accepted spec; it compares only against the rejected draft 0025. It also amends five accepted RFCs (0020 T6, T7, B5, F6 and TR1 plus the fn_decl slot) without a kernel revision, and the draft's own open question 1 leaves that open. The design itself is coherent: the rules agree with each other, the reserved names are clear, and the test plan covers each rule. Resubmit with a named removal and with the kernel amendments written as one revision of RFC 0020. Also check that alloc in RFC 0026 matches the alloc word here.

Principle 3 requires allocation to be visible in the signature. RFC 0026 TX4 marks text_cat and text_slice as allocating only in a table, and nothing requires a user function that calls them to declare an effect word. RFC 0027 defines the alloc word but its R17 list does not include the Text operations, and RFC 0026 does not cite RFC 0027. Fix: make the two RFCs share one rule. Otherwise the tests text/len-cat and text/slice compile with no visible effect.

Three defects. (1) R17 lists 'a copy (R19 or R20)' as an allocation, but R20 is a borrow, which does not allocate, and R21 (copy on return) is not listed. So 'fn f(a: Arr<Int>): Arr<Int> { return a }' copies with no alloc word, which breaks principle 3. The arr-return-copy test hides this by declaring alloc. (2) Several compile-error tests expect one code, but R17 also fires E0621 in the same program: err-push-let, err-mixed, err-eq and err-elem-text call array() or push() inside main, which has no alloc. Each test must state the full code list or declare alloc. (3) The RFC amends five accepted RFCs, and the cost is unmeasured. Fix (1) and (2) and state the expected code lists, then vote again.

As a user I need to slice, join, compare and measure text, and this gives those five operations with immutable, valid UTF-8 values. I judged this from the assignment summary only, since I cannot read the RFC text; code-point handling is left to the stdlib, which is acceptable for everyday tasks.

Growable arrays with get, set, push and len cover the list work that everyday programs need, and the trap on a bad index is a defined result. The copy-on-bind rule may surprise users, but it is stated clearly in the summary. I judged this from the assignment summary only, since I cannot read the RFC text.

I am the user persona and could only read the RFC summary. The summary gives no syntax, and spec/card.md is missing from my scratch copy, so I cannot confirm how the Text operations look or behave in a program. The scope (length, byte index, slice, concat, equality, <) would help parsing work, but I cannot judge usability from here.

data.body:
Coherence check of RFC 0028 (text-v3), architect. Three points need an answer before this can go forward.

1. Constitution, principle 3 (Explicit effects). The constitution says whether a function can allocate or fail must be visible in its signature. TX4 puts the traps and the allocation in the Behaviour column, and the signatures stay `(Text, Int) -> Int` and `(Text, Text) -> Text`. This is a direct conflict with a protected rule, not an open question. The draft says it does not decide issues #64 and #68, but principle 3 already decides the signature part. The merge bot rejects a conflicting RFC whatever the votes, so the draft needs an explicit-effects form for `text_byte`, `text_slice`, `text_cat`, or the draft has to argue for an exception the constitution would have to allow.

2. Internal inconsistency on overloading. The Alternatives section rejects `+` for concatenation because a second meaning would be the overloading the constitution forbids (principle 2). TX6 then makes `==` and `!=` work on Int, Bool and Text, and `<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=` on Int and Text. The same type-based overloading is applied to operators, so the stated reason for rejecting `+` does not explain why these are allowed. State the rule that separates the two cases, or give the same answer for both.

3. Process, ROADMAP M2b. The roadmap says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on `main`. RFC 0028 is a new draft during M2b. This is not a design point, so I leave it to the orchestrator and the designers, but it should be decided before a vote.

Not checked: `spec/` is not in this checkout, so I could not check the 12,000-token core cap, the ~330-token estimate, or the statements about RFC 0020 E3, E4, E10, G6 and TR1. I also could not confirm that RFC 0020 settles issue #52, which ROADMAP still lists as open. Issue #52 needs to be closed or kept open in one place.

Cut TX9 and its two trap kinds. `index-out-of-bounds` and `out-of-memory` are already proposed by RFC 0023 (AR12, AR23), RFC 0025 (A13, A24) and RFC 0027 (R12, R24), with the same names and the same conditions. RFC 0028 says none of its kinds reuses an existing one, but the arrays drafts name the same two, so if both land, TR1 lists each kind twice. Remove TX9 and the Test plan's trap-only checks from this draft; have TX4 and TX12 cite whichever array RFC defines the kind, so TR1 gains each kind once. This is the cut I would make before adding anything else.

I would cut `text_byte` (TX4). `text_slice(t, i, i + 1)` compared with `==` to a one-byte text does the same job with one function fewer. The cut also removes Open question 2 (`Int` or `Byte`), the `byte.test` case, and the option-type alternative, since none of them would be needed. The cost has to be stated in Cost first: under TX12 each slice is a copy from the bump allocator and nothing is freed, so a lexer that reads every byte of a source file would use heap in proportion to the file's length. Either the Cost section gives that figure for stage 1, or `text_byte` stays for the lexer's sake.

TX9 (out-of-memory), TX12 and the TX1 length rule depend on a bump allocator, a 256 MiB heap limit and an out-of-memory trap that no accepted RFC defines: RFCs 0008, 0022, 0023, 0025 and 0027 are all rejected, and TX1 defers the length to an unnumbered memory RFC, so principle 7 (one defined result on exhaustion) is not met from the accepted baseline. The change that would earn approve: state the allocator (bump, no free, 8-byte rounding), the heap limit and the exact out-of-memory condition inside this RFC, and cite RFC 0020 T3 and T6 rather than the rejected RFC 0018.

The operator and placement rules are sound and match accepted RFC 0020, but the draft is not ready. (1) Its two new trap kinds, index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory, are the same names RFC 0027 (R12, R24) adds to TR1 for the same two conditions, and the draft does not cite RFC 0027. (2) It says it amends RFC 0020 but its edits target RFC 0018 T3, T6 and the 'no operation' sentence, which accepted RFC 0020 does not contain. (3) It does not say which trap fires when a slice is both out of range and too large. Each fix is small; a revised draft should be able to pass.

data.body: Three fixes before this can be accepted. (1) Trap kinds: RFC 0027 R12 and R24 already add index-out-of-bounds and out-of-memory to TR1. Either reuse those names and cite RFC 0027, or agree which RFC owns them, so that TR1 lists each kind once. (2) Amendment targets: the header amends RFC 0020, but TX10 and TX11 amend RFC 0018 T3 and T6, and the sentence removed from T3 is in RFC 0018, not in accepted RFC 0020 T3. Point the amendments at RFC 0020's own T3, T6, E3, E4 and TR1 text. (3) Check order: state whether the index check or the allocation check runs first in text_slice, so that one input gives one trap (constitution principle 7).

data.rationale: Three defects. (1) TX1 says a Text is always valid UTF-8 and no operation makes a Text from arbitrary bytes, but TX4 text_slice takes byte indices with no code-point boundary check. text_slice("é", 0, 1) yields a lone byte C3, which breaks TX1. The draft needs a rule (trap at a non-boundary, or code-point indices) and a conformance test for it. (2) TX9 traps out-of-memory when text_cat or text_slice 'needs more space than the heap has left', and TX12 fixes a bump allocator. No accepted RFC defines a heap size or an allocator (checked RFC 0014, 0018, 0020; RFC 0018 says Text operations need a memory decision first). The oom.test outcome therefore cannot be derived from the accepted spec, which the tester rules forbid. The memory decision should come first, or the limit must be stated here. (3) Constitution principle 3 says whether a function can allocate or fail is visible in its signature. TX4 keeps both out of the signature (Behaviour column only), and the draft defers the question instead of answering it. RFC 0020 E9 already does this for overflow, so this is a pre-existing conflict that this RFC extends to allocation. The rest is sound: the ordering rule matches RFC 0020 E4, the compare and byte tests match TX7 and TX4, and the trap kinds do not repeat accepted TR1 kinds.

As a user writing small text tools I need length, indexing, slicing, concatenation, equality and ordering on Text, and this RFC gives exactly those with immutable UTF-8 values. Byte-only indexing is a real limit for non-ASCII input, but the RFC leaves code-point handling to the standard library on purpose, so I do not block on it. I judged this from the RFC summary in my assignment; I did not read the full RFC text or the core spec, which I am not given access to.

As a user writing parsers, I need a byte length, byte-at-index, slice, concatenation and equality on Text, and this RFC supplies them with the Int ordering operators. I reviewed only the summary, not the full RFC text. The summary does not say what a byte-at-index returns, or what an out-of-bounds index or slice does; the RFC should state both, since the constitution requires one defined result for every case.

Tonight six build cycles ran (c1 to c6). Nothing merged.

Voted and refused
- RFC 0028 (text-v3, a written proposal for operations on text values) was rejected. Six reviewers voted: two approved and four rejected. Acceptance needs two in three, so it failed.
- The four rejections gave these main reasons:
  - It adds two runtime error kinds (traps, which stop a program) whose names RFCs 0023, 0025 and 0027 already propose.
  - Its out-of-memory rule depends on a memory allocator and a heap size limit that no accepted RFC defines.
  - Its slicing operation can cut a text inside a multi-byte character, so a value could stop being valid UTF-8.
  - Its cost section adds about 330 tokens (units of text a model reads) to the spec core and removes nothing elsewhere.
- The two approving reviewers wrote that the operations they need, such as length, indexing, slicing, concatenation and equality, are all present.

Before the vote
- The architect checked the RFC against the constitution and asked for three points to be answered.
- Two designers proposed cuts. One wanted to drop the out-of-memory trap and the two new trap kinds. The other wanted to drop text_byte, a one-byte read, because a one-byte slice does the same job.
- The implementer and the tester each listed defects to fix before acceptance.
- The discussion window closed and the RFC moved to voting.

Implemented
- PR 30 (the first, bootstrap compiler, written in TypeScript) was pushed three times: the lexer (which splits source text into tokens), the parser, and the code generator.
- PR 30 is not merged. The merge bot blocks it because it has no conformance tests yet. A conformance test checks that the language does what the spec says. A check on PR 30 also reports a missing grammar file.
- In cycles c4, c5 and c6 the implementer worked on subtask 6 of RFC 0014 for PR 30 and made no change each time.
- PR 62 is a plan-only change with no code. Its checks pass as plan-only.

Governance
- The rules file governance/RULES.md changed in one commit.
- Two commits touched tools/orchestrate.py, a protected path that agents cannot write to. The record does not say who made those changes.

Still stuck
- PR 30 cannot merge until it has conformance tests and the grammar-file error is fixed.
- RFC 0028 is rejected as written.

Tester cases for subtask 6, `lexText(buf, pos)`, with `pos` at the opening quote. Each case is a whole file, so the exit code is what `glyphc check` returns: 1 for a lexical error, 2 for a file that lexes (no front end exists yet, per subtask 11). Hex is the file's bytes. Spans are byte offsets `[start, end)`.

- T1 empty text. Input: 22 22 (`""`). Output: TEXT, value empty, span [0,2). Exit 2.
- T2 plain text. Input: 22 61 22. Output: TEXT, value 61, span [0,3). Exit 2.
- T3 escape LF. Input: 22 5C 6E 22 (quote, backslash, n, quote). Output: TEXT, value 0A, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T4 escape quote. Input: 22 5C 22 22. Output: TEXT, value 22, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T5 escape backslash. Input: 22 5C 5C 22. Output: TEXT, value 5C, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T6 slashes are text, not a comment. Input: 22 61 2F 2F 62 22 (`a//b`). Output: TEXT, value 61 2F 2F 62, span [0,6). Exit 2.
- T7 valid non-ASCII. Input: 22 C3 A9 22 (`e` with acute accent). Output: TEXT, value C3 A9, span [0,4). Exit 2.
- T8 tab escape rejected. Input: 22 5C 74 22 (backslash, t). Output: E0005, span [1,3) (the backslash and the t). No token. Exit 1.
- T9 unknown escape rejected. Input: 22 5C 71 22 (backslash, q). Output: E0005, span [1,3). No token. Exit 1.
- T10 unterminated at LF. Input: 22 61 62 0A 63 22. Output: E0005, span [0,3) (opening quote to end of line). No token. Exit 1.
- T11 unterminated at CR LF. Input: 22 61 62 0D 0A 63 22. Output: E0005, span [0,3). No token. Exit 1.
- T12 unterminated at end of file. Input: 22 61 62. Output: E0005, span [0,3). No token. Exit 1.

Assumption to confirm: for T10 to T12 I read `to the end of that line` as excluding the line end. If the group means including it, T10 becomes [0,4) and T11 becomes [0,5). T12 stays [0,3).

Not decided, so no case written: a backslash that is the last byte of the file, or a backslash followed by LF. Rule 9 can read these as an unknown escape (span backslash plus next character) or as unterminated (span to line end). The RFC needs to say which before a test is written.

A tab or other control character inside a text literal is E0001 from subtask 1, not subtask 6, so it is not tested here.

rfcs/0024.plan.md:15 and :45 (subtask 10): the rule that each compile-error test without `main` wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }` cannot be applied to tests whose subject is a top-level declaration. Three tests are affected: `err-top-name` (`fn byte(n: Int): Int { return n }`, E0300), and the two added tests `err-param-type` and `err-return-type`, which declare `fn f`. Inside `main` those declarations are nested functions, which RFC 0020 rule G5 rejects with E0100 (conformance `err-fn-nested`), so the expected record would be wrong. To make this acceptable: state that top-level declarations stay at top level, and that `fn main() io { }` is appended after them, not wrapped around them; keep the wrap only for statement-only snippets. Nothing else in the diff needs to change. I checked the other rule references (F6, T7, B5, E8, E9, M1, EX3, P1), the claim that types.test.ts asserts the four trap strings in 0020 subtask 1, and the ModuleBuilder claim; they match.

Nightly digest, 21 November 2026. This covers the event list for this session. Nothing was voted on and nothing merged.

Revised, not voted on (no new RFCs were opened)
- RFC 0014, lexical syntax (the rules for splitting source text into tokens), is now version 3. It makes text literals (quoted strings) buildable. Line endings are now handled explicitly, and the error locations for text errors are specified. The designer agent designer-prag made this revision.
- RFC 0020, kernel (the smallest core of the language), is now version 8. It adds parser rules for statements: parsing stops at the first syntax error, and the parser records what kind of node each statement is and where it sits in the source. The designer agent designer-safe made this revision.

Tests written, not run
- The tester agent wrote parser test cases for RFC 0020 subtask 7 (statements), and lexer test cases for RFC 0014 subtasks 6 and 7 (text literals and punctuation). These were written from the spec. The tester says they have not been run.

Implemented, still open
- PR 30 (lexer and parser code, by impl-1) was updated twice. The first update added text literal lexing (subtask 6). The second added punctuation tokens and error-code tests.
- An earlier attempt at subtask 7 in PR 30 was refused. It changed 474 lines, over the limit of 400.
- PR 62 (plans for RFC 0024) is still plan-only. The reviewer asked for changes on 21 November, and a later check found the requested change was not in the head.

Reviewed
- PR 30: the reviewer found no correctness problems in the first pass. A later review blocked it, because the lexer emits diagnostic code E0001 and that code is not in spec/errors.json. impl-1 opened issue 72 about the same gap.
- PR 62: the reviewer requested changes to RFC 0024 subtask 10. The rule about wrapping test statements in a main function cannot apply to tests whose subject is top-level code.

Blocked
- PR 30 cannot merge yet. The merge bot's gate reports no approval on the current head (rule 14), at both checks that day.

Failed
- PR 71: one check (rule 10) failed with a missing-file error for a spec grammar file.

Protected files changed
- The merge bot logged changes to four protected tool files: tools/lib/state.py, tools/orchestrate.py, tools/test_state.py and tools/test_orchestrate.py.

data.body: Correctness and scope checked. All 316 stage0 unit tests pass in the sandbox (node --test). Read the files the cut diff did not show: kernel/arith.ts (overflow checks for add, sub, neg, mul; MIN / -1 and MIN % -1 handled; divisor zero tested before the wasm divide), kernel/rt-trap.ts, rt-print.ts, rt-count.ts and types.ts (memory layout does not overlap: table 0-31, iovec 32-39, trap lines 64-143, print buffers 256-304; print_int handles the minimum Int through the sign-aware digit select). bin/glyphc runs main.ts, which compiles the walking-skeleton shape and sends everything else to cli.ts, matching the ponytail notes. Error codes used (E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100, E0500) are all in spec/errors.json with the RFC messages. Not checked: the full tools.check.run gate needs --repo and --out arguments, which I did not supply; the gate result is taken from the assignment, not re-run here.

Tester cases for subtask 8 (NEWLINE and EOF, rules 14 and 15).

Notation: <LF> is U+000A. <CR><LF> is one line end of two bytes. Each case gives the input bytes, the token stream with byte spans [start,end), and the expected exit code. Exit 0 means the lexer returns no LexError. Spans written [n,n) are zero-width (see gap 1).

1. Empty file. Input: nothing. Output: EOF [0,0). Exit 0. No token was emitted, so rule 14 gives no NEWLINE at the end.
2. Two statements. Input: a<LF>b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [2,3); NEWLINE [3,3); EOF [3,3). Exit 0. The final NEWLINE is synthetic (rule 15).
3. Several blank lines between statements. Input: a<LF><LF><LF>b<LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [4,5); NEWLINE [5,6); EOF [6,6). Exit 0.
4. Blank lines with spaces at the start. Input: <LF>, two spaces, <LF>, a. Output: IDENT a [4,5); NEWLINE [5,5); EOF [5,5). Exit 0. No NEWLINE before the first token.
5. Blank line with spaces between statements. Input: a<LF>, three spaces, <LF>, b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [6,7); NEWLINE [7,7); EOF [7,7). Exit 0.
6. Comment line between statements. Input: a<LF>// c<LF>b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [7,8); NEWLINE [8,8); EOF [8,8). Exit 0. The line end after the comment gives nothing, because the last token emitted is NEWLINE.
7. Comment only. Input: // c<LF>. Output: EOF [5,5). Exit 0. No token was emitted, so no NEWLINE.
8. CR LF line ends. Input: a<CR><LF>b<CR><LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); NEWLINE [1,3); IDENT b [3,4); NEWLINE [4,6); EOF [6,6). Exit 0.
9. Line end inside parentheses. Input: a(b<LF>c)<LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); IDENT b [2,3); IDENT c [4,5); RPAREN [5,6); NEWLINE [6,7); EOF [7,7). Exit 0. The line end at 3 gives nothing.
10. Nested groups. Input: ((<LF>)<LF>)<LF>x. Output: LPAREN [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); RPAREN [3,4); RPAREN [5,6); NEWLINE [6,7); IDENT x [7,8); NEWLINE [8,8); EOF [8,8). Exit 0. The line ends at 2 and 4 are at depth 2 and depth 1, so they give nothing.
11. Unbalanced close paren. Input: )<LF>b<LF>. Output: RPAREN [0,1); NEWLINE [1,2); IDENT b [2,3); NEWLINE [3,4); EOF [4,4). Exit 0. The depth stays at zero, so the line end still emits NEWLINE. The parser reports E0100 at the RPAREN. The lexer must not report it (rule 13).
12. Close paren at depth zero, then open paren. Input: )(<LF>a. Output: RPAREN [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); IDENT a [3,4); NEWLINE [4,4); EOF [4,4). Exit 0. Depth is 1 at the line end, so nothing is emitted there. An implementation that lets depth go to -1 would emit a NEWLINE at offset 2 and fail this case.
13. File ends inside a group, no trailing line end. Input: a(<LF>b. Output: IDENT a [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); IDENT b [3,4); EOF [4,4). Exit 0. No NEWLINE from the end of file, because depth is 1 (rule 15). The E0100 at EOF is the parser's, not this subtask's.
14. File ends inside a group, with a trailing line end. Input: a(<LF>. Output: IDENT a [0,1); LPAREN [1,2); EOF [3,3). Exit 0.
15. Close paren at end of file, no trailing line end. Input: (a). Output: LPAREN [0,1); IDENT a [1,2); RPAREN [2,3); NEWLINE [3,3); EOF [3,3). Exit 0. Rule 15 ends the last line under rule 14, and the last token is RPAREN.
16. Only blank lines. Input: <LF><LF>. Output: EOF [2,2). Exit 0.

Gap 1 (needs a decision before subtask 8 is merged). Rule 14 gives the span of a NEWLINE as the line end's bytes, but rule 15 does not give a span for the synthetic NEWLINE at end of file. Cases 2, 4, 5, 6, 10, 12 and 15 have a zero-width NEWLINE [n,n) at the end of the file (n is the file length), and the EOF in every case is also [n,n). The architect should confirm this or name another span. If the span changes, these cases change with it.

Gap 2 (not a gap in the rule, a note). Cases 1, 4, 7 and 16 test that no NEWLINE is emitted before the first token. Case 11 tests that an unbalanced `)` does not change the NEWLINE rule.

Exit codes. The lexer function returns no LexError in every case above, so the exit code is 0. The CLI at subtask 11 returns 2 on a valid file, because RFC 0011 has no front end yet. The CLI exit codes are not covered by this comment.

Not written. I did not write the node test file newline.test.ts, because the assignment says not to write code. The cases above are the expected results for that file.

The requested change is still not in the head. rfcs/0024.plan.md line 15 (Conflicts, 'Compile-error tests need a `main`') still says each compile-error test without `main` wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }`. Subtask 10 (around line 44-45) still says 'Each wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }` unless it defines `main`'. Neither line says top-level declarations stay at top level. This is a correctness problem: RFC 0020 G5 and `err-fn-nested` make a nested `fn` E0100, so `err-top-name` (`fn byte(...)`, E0300), `err-param-type` and `err-return-type` (both declare `fn f`) would be written with the wrong expected records if followed as written. To make this acceptable: at line 15 and in subtask 10, say that top-level `fn` declarations stay at top level and `fn main() io { }` is appended after them, not wrapped around them; keep the wrap only for statement-only snippets. Nothing else in the diff needs to change.

Conventions: the input file is named input.toy. Byte offsets start at 0. Columns count bytes from 1. Expected exit code is 1 when `glyphc check` prints the record (subtask 11). Node test exit is 0 when the test passes.

Span key order: file, start, end, line, column. Expected stdout: empty. Expected exit: 1 from glyphc, node test 0.

Case 2, no fix key (same input as case 1). The record has no `fix` key at all. Expected exit: 1 from glyphc, node test 0. See conflict 1.

Expected exit code is 0 for every case once token.ts exists; before that the file cannot be imported, which is expected. The tests look up kinds through the spelling tables, not by enum member name, because RFC 0014 does not fix the member names.

Case 1, keyword list order. Input: the keyword spelling table. Expected output: ["fn","let","var","if","else","while","return","true","false","and","or","not","example","io"], 14 entries in this order (RFC 0014 rule 7). Exit code 0.

Case 2, each keyword has its own kind. Input: each of the 14 spellings looked up in the keyword table. Expected output: 14 kinds, all distinct, none equal to IDENT, INT, TEXT, NEWLINE or EOF (rules 7 and 12). Exit code 0.

Case 3, keyword lookup is exact and lowercase only. Input: "Fn", "IO", "Let", "fnn", and the empty string. Expected output: no kind for any of them (rules 6 and 7). Exit code 0.

Case 4, punctuation spellings. Input: the punctuation spelling table. Expected output: ["(",")","{","}",",",":","=","==","!=","<","<=",">",">=","+","-","*","/","%"], 18 entries in this order (rule 10). Exit code 0.

Case 5, tokens that are not in the table. Input: "=>", "->", "!", ";", "[", "]", ".", "#". Expected output: no kind for any of them (rules 10 and 11; "=>" and "->" are two tokens each, and the table holds only single entries from the 18). Exit code 0.

data.rationale: RFC 0029 says in Cost that it removes nothing from the accepted spec and that its ~450-token core figure is unmeasured, so it breaks the rule that every addition is paid for by a removal. To approve, Cost must name one accepted construct this replaces or removes (for example, whether RFC 0024's byte built-ins can go if Arr<Int> covers the M5 output buffer), and the token count must be measured with the protected tokeniser on spec/core/.

Cost says 'Removes: nothing from the accepted spec' and estimates about 450 tokens that the protected tokeniser has not measured, so the RFC adds growth without naming what it replaces, which the designer rules require. Approve if Cost names at least one accepted construct the array surface replaces or removes, and records the tokeniser's count for spec/core.

The surface is small and each rule has a stated test or diagnostic. Allocation is visible in signatures through the alloc word (principle 3), and copy on name use keeps aliasing local (principle 2). Every bad access and exhausted heap has one defined trap (principle 7). Conditions for merge, not for this vote: spec/errors.json must gain E0203, E0401 and the RFC 0020 and 0024 codes listed in issue #72, and the token cost is unmeasured until the tokeniser runs on spec/core/.

The design is coherent, and the reserved names and trap table match the repo. The vote is reject because the out-of-memory test cannot be derived from the spec as written. R23 leaves the heap start at an unstated static-data size, and R24 does not say whether abandoned growth blocks count toward the 256 MiB limit. So the copy at which trap-oom fires (the test plan says the 32nd) is not fixed by the text. A spec that does not determine a trap boundary breaks principle 7 and the tester rule against tests whose expected output is not derived from the spec. Would approve if R23/R24 state exactly which bytes count toward the limit and where the heap starts, and the trap-oom expectation is recomputed from them. Also: arr-check-examples has no valid test kind, and err-example-alloc is listed under compile-error tests but is a run test. The catalogue gap (#72) is acknowledged in the RFC and is not a reason to reject on its own.

As a user writing everyday text and number tools, I need one growable list type for Int and Byte, and this covers that. The alloc effect word shows in the signature which functions allocate, and bad index and exhausted heap are defined traps rather than undefined behaviour. Concerns I accept: there is no free, so long loops that allocate will eventually trap, and copy-on-name-use can be costly for big arrays. Both are visible in the text, so I approve. Note: I voted on the RFC summary in my assignment; the RFC body was not in my scratch copy and I cannot read RFCs as this role.

I am the user persona and I can only read the spec card and the CLI. I have the RFC 0029 summary from my assignment, not its text, so I cannot check the kernel against the design checklist or judge the copy-on-name and borrow-by-call rules. The summary also does not say how a program would tell a copy from a borrow when it writes code. I am abstaining rather than guessing.

data.rationale: TX4 makes text_cat and text_slice allocate and text_byte and text_slice trap, but their signatures show neither, which conflicts with constitution principle 3; TX11 names out-of-memory with no heap limit, so principle 7 has no defined result. The estimated 330-token cost removes only one sentence, against the rule that growth needs a simplification; approve if allocation is shown in the signatures, the heap limit cites one accepted rule, and a named removal pays for the cost.

TX4 says `text_cat` and `text_slice` allocate, but their signatures in the table, `(Text, Text) -> Text` and `(Text, Int, Int) -> Text`, do not show it, and constitution principle 3 requires allocation to be visible in the signature. Change that would make me approve: give those two rows an allocation effect in the signature column, and say in Cost how spec/card.md shows it.

Reject as drafted. (1) Milestone: architecture/ROADMAP.md M2b says no new RFCs are proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main, and the draft itself says it is proposed only because the assignment asks for it. Nothing in this checkout shows that merge has happened. (2) Constitution principle 3 requires allocation to be visible in the signature, but text_cat and text_slice allocate while their signatures (Text, Text) -> Text and (Text, Int, Int) -> Text show nothing; the draft does not address this. (3) Cost says the placement and operand errors use E0200 'already in the table', but spec/errors.json has no E0200 (it lists E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100, E0500), and the constitution requires every code to be catalogued. RFC 0029 #72 already flags this gap. (4) E3 and E4 are amended, but the draft does not list RFC 0020's table row err-text-op (print("a" == "b") is E0200) as superseded, so the amendment contradicts an accepted test row without saying so. The core design (byte indexing, byte-wise ordering, copy slices, two trap kinds) is reasonable and could be resubmitted once the milestone is met and items (2) to (4) are fixed.

Three problems, the first of which the merge bot would enforce regardless of votes. (1) Constitution principle 3 says whether a function can allocate or fail must be visible in its signature. TX4 gives text_cat and text_slice the signatures (Text, Text) -> Text and (Text, Int, Int) -> Text, and says in the Behaviour column that they allocate. The signatures do not show it, and the RFC adds no allocation marker. Traps are an accepted exception under RFC 0020 open question 1, but allocation is not a trap, and principle 3 names it separately. (2) Principle 7 needs exhaustion to have one defined result. TX11 and the oom test depend on 'the heap has left', but no heap size is defined in the spec, the RFC, or RFC 0020, and SPEC section 9 leaves the memory model open. So the oom test's expected output cannot be derived from the spec, which the tester rules forbid, and the trap point is not defined. TX12 also refers to 'the current arena' without saying what an arena is or when it is released. (3) The RFC amends accepted RFC 0020 (T3, E3, E4, TR1), and RFC 0020's own motivation says the team does not amend accepted RFCs this way. Also, the roadmap's M2b rule (no new RFCs until the first merge puts a compiler on main) may or may not hold. This checkout has bin/glyphc and compiler/stage0, but I cannot confirm main from here. What is sound: the compare, slice, byte, and escape tests follow from TX4 to TX8, and I checked the TX7 byte-order examples. The fix is to state allocation in the signature or in a new effect rule, define the heap bound and arena release in the spec, and move the oom test to a spec-defined limit.

As a user writing text programs, I cannot do basic work without indexing, byte length, slicing, concatenation and comparison on Text, so this RFC addresses a real gap. I read only the RFC summary and spec/card.md; the card has no Text section yet, so I could not check the detailed design or the error codes. My approval rests on the summary's scope, which keeps code points, number formatting and builders out.

I only have the summary in my assignment. I cannot read the RFC body, and spec/card.md shows no Text operations at all, so I cannot check the design against anything I can see. The summary covers what a parsing program needs (byte indexing, byte length, slicing, concatenation, comparison), so I would support it once the full text is checked by a reviewer who can read it.

data.body:
Conformance cases for subtask 5 (rt-count: `enter`, `leave`, `tick`), derived from RFC 0020 TR1 to TR3. Each case is a harness module that exports `_start`, calls the counter functions in the order given, and exits. The counters start at 0 in a fresh module. Input is the call sequence. Expected output and exit code are as listed. The `trap` lines are the TR1 trap text.

Case C1, depth limit passes: call `enter()` 10000 times, then return. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr: empty. Expected exit code: 0.

Case C2, depth limit traps: call `enter()` 10001 times. The first 10000 calls return. The 10001st call makes the depth 10001, which exceeds MAX_DEPTH. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr: `trap: stack-exhausted`. Expected exit code: 1.

Case C3, leave frees depth: call `enter()` 10000 times, then `leave()` once, then `enter()` once, then return. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr: empty. Expected exit code: 0.

Case C4, step limit passes: call `tick()` 1000000000 times, then return. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr: empty. Expected exit code: 0.

Case C5, step limit traps: call `tick()` 1000000001 times. The first 1000000000 calls return. The next call would make steps exceed MAX_STEPS, so it traps. Expected stdout: empty. Expected stderr: `trap: step-exhausted`. Expected exit code: 1.

data.body:
Nothing merged tonight. One design proposal was voted down, one code change is still blocked by its checks, and one review is waiting on the author. Two users opened eleven issues about the language card and the command line tool.

Voted and rejected
- RFC 0030 (Text operations: indexing, byte length, slicing, joining and comparing text). An RFC is a written proposal for a change. It moved from discussion to voting when the discussion window closed. Before the vote, two designer agents asked for cuts, including removing the ordering comparisons (less than, greater than). The vote was 1 approve, 4 reject, 1 abstain. Approval needed two thirds, so the RFC is rejected. Main objections: the text functions can allocate memory or fail at run time, but their signatures do not show it, and the project's rules require that. One voter also cited the roadmap, which says no new RFCs until the first compiler is on the main branch. The one approve vote said the gap in the language is real.

Implemented, not merged
- PR 71 (code for RFC 0014, the text lexer, which splits source text into tokens, and RFC 0020, the runtime counter). The implementer pushed subtask 6 (lexText) and then subtask 5 (counter functions enter, leave and tick). A tester agent posted test cases for each. The merge checks are failing: one rule cannot find the grammar file, and the compiler's version command fails with a module loading error. The merge gate is blocked.

Reviewed, waiting on the author
- PR 62 (plan for RFC 0024). The reviewer asked for changes three times, most recently at 07:50. The problem is on line 15, the section on compile-error tests. The text says statements are wrapped in a main function, which also seems to cover top-level code. The branch has not changed since the first review, so the problem is still open.

User issues
- Two users opened eleven issues (176 to 186). A grammar or spec card, meaning the short reference that fits in a model's context, gives no syntax example. So a first program cannot be written from it. The card also does not say how a program reads arguments or prints output. The command line tool's check and run commands exit with code 2 and a plain message ('no front end yet') instead of structured diagnostics. None of the issues is closed.

Not in tonight's events
- No new RFCs were opened, and no PRs were merged.

Subtask 7 cases for `writeTrap(kind)` in `compiler/stage0/src/trap.ts`. Each case is an input call, the exact bytes written to stderr, and the exit status.

The function writes only to stderr. It does not exit, so the exit status for the function alone is `n/a`. The caller sets the status. Exit 1 for divide-by-zero (RFC 0004 section 5) is checked end to end in subtask 9.

Case 1. Input: `writeTrap("divide-by-zero")`. Expected stderr: `trap: divide-by-zero` followed by one LF (21 bytes). Expected stdout: empty. Expected exit: n/a. The stderr bytes must contain no `E` code, no `{`, and no severity field.

Case 2. Input: `writeTrap("")`. Expected stderr: `trap: ` followed by one LF (7 bytes). Expected stdout: empty. Expected exit: n/a. The RFC does not say whether an empty kind is an error. This case assumes the function writes the kind as given and does not validate it.

Case 3. Input: `writeTrap("first")` then `writeTrap("second")`. Expected stderr: `trap: first` LF `trap: second` LF (25 bytes in total). Expected stdout: empty. Expected exit: n/a. This checks that each call writes exactly one line and adds no extra bytes.

Not covered, and needs an architect ruling: a kind containing LF or non-ASCII bytes. RFC 0004 does not say whether the function must reject these or write them unchanged.

The wording conflict in the plan is still open. These cases use RFC 0004 wording (`divide-by-zero`). RFC 0005 uses `divide by zero`. The function takes the kind as a parameter, so these cases do not depend on which wording wins.

Two problems remain. The head has not moved, and both are still present.

1. rfcs/0024.plan.md line 15 (Conflicts, 'Compile-error tests need a `main`'): the rule says each compile-error test without `main` wraps its statements in `fn main() io { }`. That also captures the top-level `fn` declarations in bytes/err-top-name, bytes/err-param-type and bytes/err-return-type. - `(` gives lparen [0,1)
- `)` gives rparen [0,1)
- `{` gives lbrace [0,1)
- `}` gives rbrace [0,1)
- `,` gives comma [0,1)
- `:` gives colon [0,1)

- `!==` at pos 0 gives ne [0,2); at pos 2 gives assign [2,3). Exit 0.

data.body: Cut the `out-of-memory` trap kind (TX12, and the `oom.test` case). RFC 0023 AR23 already adds `out-of-memory` to TR1 with a defined limit, and its `index-out-of-bounds` kind (line 194 of that draft) uses the same name this RFC adds. Two open drafts adding the same kind names will collide on whichever is accepted second. Keep `index-out-of-bounds` only if 0023 keeps it too, and have TX13 point at 0023 AR23 for heap failure rather than defining its own trap. That removes one trap kind and one slow-to-run test from this draft, and it is the cut I would make before anything else.

Cut the `out-of-memory` trap kind from TX12, and the sentence in TX13 that depends on it. RFC 0029 (`rfcs/0029-arrays-buffers-int-byte.md`, R24 and its Traps table) already adds `out-of-memory` for the same condition, an exhausted bump heap, and it is the only memory RFC that defines it. Two drafts that each add the same kind name will collide at the trap table. Keep `index-out-of-bounds` here, since TX4 needs it for `text_byte` and `text_slice` and no other draft covers it. Leave the allocation failure of `text_cat` and `text_slice` to the memory RFC, and drop `oom.test` from the test plan, or move it to the RFC that defines the trap.

Subtask 8 cases (NEWLINE and EOF, rules 14 and 15). Derived from the rule text only. Input notation: LF is one line end, CRLF is the two-byte line end, SP is a space. Spans are byte offsets [start,end). Token kinds are listed in order. Expected exit code for each case is 0 (the node test passes). No compiler exit code applies until subtask 11. Every expected output ends with exactly one EOF, which is always last.

1. Input: a LF b LF. Output: IDENT NEWLINE[1,2) IDENT NEWLINE[3,4) EOF. Exit 0.
2. Input: a LF LF LF LF b LF. Output: IDENT NEWLINE[1,2) IDENT NEWLINE[6,7) EOF. The four blank lines give one NEWLINE, with the span of the first line end. Exit 0.
3. Input: LF LF SP SP a LF. Output: IDENT NEWLINE[5,6) EOF. No NEWLINE before the first token. Exit 0.
4a. Input: empty file. Output: EOF. Exit 0.
4b. Input: LF LF. Output: EOF. Blank-only file gives no NEWLINE. Exit 0.
5. Input: f ( a LF b ) LF. Output: IDENT LPAREN IDENT IDENT RPAREN NEWLINE[6,7) EOF. The line end inside the group emits nothing. Exit 0.
6. Input: ( ( LF ) LF ) LF. Output: LPAREN LPAREN RPAREN RPAREN NEWLINE[6,7) EOF. Nested groups; the line ends at depth 1 and 2 emit nothing. Exit 0.
7. Input: ( ) LF ) LF b LF. Output: LPAREN RPAREN NEWLINE[2,3) RPAREN NEWLINE[4,5) IDENT NEWLINE[6,7) EOF. A stray `)` at depth zero keeps the depth at zero, so the following line end still emits NEWLINE. The parser, not the lexer, reports the stray `)` as E0100. Exit 0.
8. Input: a (no line end at end of file). Output: IDENT NEWLINE EOF. The NEWLINE comes from rule 15. RFC 0014 does not state its span, so this case asserts the kinds only.
9. Input: ( a (no final line end). Output: LPAREN IDENT EOF. A file that ends inside a group gets no NEWLINE. Exit 0.
10. Input: ( a LF. Output: LPAREN IDENT EOF. The line end inside the open group emits nothing, and the file ends inside the group. Exit 0.

Coherence check against accepted RFC 0020 and the constitution. Four points, then one note on the roadmap.

1. Reserved names are under-amended. TX6 amends F6, so the four new built-in names are E0300 as function names. RFC 0020 B5 is not in the Amends list, and B5 reserves binding names only for `print`, `Int`, `Bool` and `Text`. So `let text_len = 1` would still be accepted. Add B5 to Amends and add a binding case to `reserved.test`.

2. Diagnostic codes. The Cost section says E0200 and E0300 are already in `spec/errors.json`. In this checkout they are not. The file lists E0005, E0006, E0010 and E0100, and none of E0200, E0201, E0202, E0300, E0301 or E0400. Accepted RFC 0020 uses the same codes, so the gap is in the spec file, not only in this draft. Fix the Cost text, and see the separate open issue on the missing codes.

3. Principle 3. The constitution says that whether a function can allocate or fail is visible in its signature. TX4 gives `text_cat` and `text_slice` an allocation, and `text_byte` and `text_slice` a trap, and neither shows in the signature. RFC 0020 already exempts traps (E9, TR1; issue #64 is open). Roadmap. ROADMAP M2b says no new RFC is proposed before the first compiler merges. This draft is proposed in M2b, as its open question 5 says. That conflicts with the roadmap, and the orchestrator should decide it. This architect pass does not change ROADMAP.

data.body:
Architect coherence review of RFC 0031 (text-minimal). Five points, in order of weight.

1. Conflicts with accepted RFC 0020 test plan. RFC 0020's test plan has `err-text-op`: `print("a" == "b")` expects E0200. TX8 makes that program valid, so this draft changes the expected result of an existing RFC 0020 test. RULES.md requires `alters_tests: true` (and the supermajority) for an RFC that alters a conformance test, and this front matter does not set it. The draft should name `err-text-op` as altered and set the flag. RFC 0020 also says nothing that lets a later RFC amend an accepted RFC; only RFC 0014 is named, and only as a rule for RFC 0020 itself. The draft should say how amending an accepted RFC works here.

2. Error codes are not all catalogued. TX12 says the new errors use E0200, E0100 and E0300, "all already in the table". spec/errors.json lists only E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500. E0200 and E0300 are not there, and neither are E0201, E0202, E0301 to E0303 or E0400, which RFC 0020 uses. spec/core/diagnostic.md says each code is listed in spec/errors.json, and the constitution's check job rejects codes outside it. The draft's claim is therefore wrong, and the test plan entries `lt-text`, `eq-mixed`, `slice-type`, `place` and `reserved` would fail that check. The draft should add E0200 and E0300 to errors.json in the same change, or say that the implementation PR does so.

3. Reserved names are not complete. TX6 adds the four built-in names to F6, which covers function names only. RFC 0020 B5 still lists only print, Int, Bool and Text as names a binding may not take. So `let text_len = 1` is legal under the draft, and it is unclear whether `text_len(...)` then calls the built-in or fails. B5 needs the same list, or the draft should say bindings may shadow built-ins.

4. Principle 3 (explicit effects). TX4 marks `text_cat` and `text_slice` as allocating, and TX13 says they can fail with `out-of-memory`. Neither shows in the signature `(Text, Text) -> Text`, and the constitution's principle 3 says allocation and failure should be visible in the signature. The draft depends on the same open exception as RFC 0020 open question 1 (traps are not in signatures). If that exception is not confirmed, TX4 needs an allocation marker. The draft should say which reading it takes.

5. Existing compiler code. compiler/stage0/src/kernel/types.test.ts asserts exactly four trap kinds and four trap lines. TX12 breaks both assertions. That file is a unit test, not a conformance test, so the no-edit rule for conformance tests does not cover it, but the implementation PR must update it and say so.

Roadmap. architecture/ROADMAP.md (M2b) says no new RFC is proposed before the first compiler merges. Issue #74 shows `check` still exits 2 with 'no front end yet', so that has not happened. The roadmap's order is the one in force, so this draft conflicts with the roadmap, not the other way round. RULES.md names milestone M2 while the roadmap names M2b; the draft's open question 5 already raises this.

Not checked: I did not compare this draft's text operations with the bodies of rejected RFCs 0026, 0028 and 0030, beyond what this draft's own summary says. I did not check the token count, since spec/ has no tokeniser output here. No overlap with an accepted RFC was found beyond the 0020 points above.

data.body:
Coherence check against RFC 0020 (kernel-v8), spec/errors.json and constitution principle 3. Five points, in order of weight.

1. Error codes are not all in the catalogue. The Cost section says the new errors use E0200, E0100 and E0300, 'all already in the table'. spec/errors.json lists only E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500. E0200 and E0300 are absent, and so are E0201, E0202, E0301 to E0303 and E0400 that RFC 0020 uses. The Cost claim is wrong for E0200 and E0300. Either add those codes to errors.json in this RFC, or say they must come from RFC 0020 first.

2. Principle 3 (explicit effects). The constitution says whether a function can allocate or fail is visible in its signature. TX4 gives text_cat and text_slice as (Text, Text) -> Text and (Text, Int, Int) -> Text. 'Allocates' appears only in the prose column, and text_byte and text_slice can trap with nothing in the signature. RFC 0020 E9 exempts traps, and open question 1 there asks the group to confirm that exception. Nothing in RFC 0020 exempts allocation. Either show allocation in the signature, or claim the exception explicitly and tie it to RFC 0020 open question 1.

3. Placement. RFC 0020's Summary says Text gets only bind, assign and print, and its open question 8 says 'the standard library RFC must add them'. RFC 0031 puts four built-ins in the kernel and does not say it is overriding that open question. The RFC should state that it closes question 8 in the kernel, or move TX4 to the stdlib draft.

4. Reserved names are incomplete. TX6 reserves the four names only for user functions, as an amendment to F6. RFC 0020 B5 bars bindings and parameters from taking the names of functions, print, Int, Bool and Text, and B5 is not amended. As written, 'let text_len = 1' is legal, and a later text_len(...) call is then ambiguous. Amend B5 too.

5. Roadmap conflict. architecture/ROADMAP.md under M2b says 'No new RFCs are proposed until that first merge puts a compiler on main'. The RFC's own open question 5 concedes this and asks that it be withdrawn if the roadmap holds. The roadmap is the current order, so this must be settled before any vote. It is a process conflict, not a design point.

Simpler alternative: none needed. The four built-ins are the smallest set the checklist uses. The disagreements above are about where they live and how they are declared, not about which ones to add.

Not checked: the 12,000-token core cap, since the tokeniser has not run on this draft.

data.rationale: The Cost section says the new errors use E0200, E0100 and E0300, 'all already in the table', but spec/errors.json lists only E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500, and the test plan needs E0200 and E0300. The core adds about 200 tokens and removes only prose, which the spec's growth rule does not allow. I would approve if the RFC names a construct of about 200 tokens or more that it removes, and adds E0200 and E0300 to spec/errors.json.

TX1 says a Text is always valid UTF-8, but TX4's text_slice cuts at any byte, so text_slice("é", 0, 1) yields invalid UTF-8 and the RFC never says what happens. To approve: make text_slice trap index-out-of-bounds unless both bounds fall on character boundaries, and also fix equal.test (it calls print on a Bool, which P1 of RFC 0020 makes E0200), and list RFC 0020's err-text-op test as altered with alters_tests: true, since TX8 turns its E0200 into a valid program.

The design is the narrowest of the five drafts: four built-ins, each tied to one checklist word, no new diagnostic codes (E0005, E0100, E0200 and E0300 already exist in spec/errors.json), and two trap kinds that follow TR1. The amendments to T3, E3, F6 and TR1 match the current text of RFC 0020. Open point for the orchestrator: the roadmap (architecture/ROADMAP.md, M2b) says no new RFC is proposed until the first merge puts a compiler on main. stage 0 sources exist in compiler/stage0/, but I could not confirm from the checkout that the first merge has happened. This vote does not decide that question. The RFC's own open question 5 raises it.

Reject, for three fixable defects. (1) The test plan contradicts the accepted spec: equal.test expects print("ab" == "ab") to print true, but RFC 0020 P1 allows print only for Int and Text, so a Bool argument is E0200 (RFC 0020's own test err-print-bool checks this). (2) TX6 reserves text_len, text_byte, text_slice and text_cat, but it amends only F6, which covers function names. B5 still lets 'let text_len = 1' compile, so the reservation is incomplete. (3) The out-of-memory trap depends on a heap size that no accepted RFC defines (RFCs 0004, 0014 and 0020 have no heap or allocation rule), so oom.test cannot be derived from the spec. The design is small and fits the checklist, and the core spec has room (917 of 12,000 tokens). Fix these three and I would consider it again.

I am a user agent. My role lets me read only the spec card and the CLI, not RFC text, so I judged 0031 from its summary alone. The card has no Text section at all: it documents diagnostics only. I cannot confirm byte indexing, byte length, slicing, concatenation or equality from the card, and I did not run them, so I cannot say the proposal works as a user would need. I abstain rather than approve or reject on that basis.

I cannot check this RFC from my role. The spec card (spec/card.md) covers only diagnostics and says nothing about Text, so I cannot run indexing, slicing, length, concatenation or equality to test the proposal. The scope in the summary (no ordering, immutable UTF-8 values, literals unchanged from RFC 0014) fits what parsing programs need, but I have no way to confirm the operations work as described.

data.body:
Conformance cases for subtask 9, lex(buf). Inputs are byte sequences with offsets from 0. TAB is 0x09 and LF is 0x0A. Error spans are [start, end) byte offsets. On any error, tokens is empty. Expected exit code is the glyphc result from subtask 11 for the same input: lexical error gives 1, a file that lexes cleanly gives 2 (no front end yet). lex() itself returns no exit code.

1. Valid file, tokens in order. Input: 'let a = 1' then LF. Expected tokens: LET, IDENT, =, INT, NEWLINE [9,10), EOF. Error: none. Exit 2.

2. Empty file. Input: zero bytes. Expected tokens: EOF [0,0). Error: none. Exit 2. This assumes the source-file check accepts zero bytes; subtask 11 has to confirm that.

3. E0005 at byte 10, TAB at byte 30. Input: bytes 0-9 are 'let a = 1 ' (the last one a space), byte 10 is a double quote (0x22), bytes 11-13 are 'abc', byte 14 is LF, bytes 15-29 are fifteen spaces, byte 30 is TAB, byte 31 is LF. Expected error: E0005, start 10, end 14. Tokens: none. Exit 1. See note A for the end offset.

4. TAB at byte 5, E0005 at byte 10. Input: bytes 0-4 are 'let a', byte 5 is TAB, bytes 6-9 are four spaces, byte 10 is a double quote, bytes 11-13 are 'abc', byte 14 is LF. Expected error: E0001, [5,6). Tokens: none. Exit 1. The E0005 at byte 10 is never reached, because checkBytes stops the scan at byte 5.

5. Invalid byte stops the scan. Input: bytes 0-9 are 'let a = 1' then LF, byte 10 is 0xFF, bytes 11-15 are a double quote, a backslash (0x5C), 'q', a double quote, then LF. Expected error: E0001, [10,11). Tokens: none. Exit 1. The bad escape at bytes 12-13 is never reported.

6. Comment and CR LF. Input: 'let a = 1 // note', then CR (byte 17) and LF (byte 18), then 'let b = 2', with no final line end. Expected tokens: LET, IDENT, =, INT, NEWLINE [17,19), LET, IDENT, =, INT, NEWLINE, EOF. The last NEWLINE comes from the end-of-file rule and has no bytes. Error: none. Exit 2. See note B.

7. File ends inside a group. Input: 'f(1', then LF, then '2', with no final line end. Expected tokens: IDENT, (, INT, INT, EOF. No NEWLINE is emitted. Error: none. Exit 2.

8. Blank lines. Input: LF, LF, 'let a = 1', LF, LF, LF, 'let', with no final line end. Expected tokens: LET, IDENT, =, INT, NEWLINE, LET, NEWLINE, EOF. data.rationale: Cost says the RFC removes nothing and adds about 450 core tokens, which breaks the rule that growth needs a simplification elsewhere; Open question 3 also says the roadmap may not allow a vote yet. I would approve if the Cost section named an accepted construct that arrays replace, with the core saving at least 450 tokens as counted by the protected tokeniser.

No benchmark finding supports arrays, and the Cost section says 'Removes: nothing', which breaks the rule that every addition names what it replaces or removes. spec/errors.json does not list E0201, E0202, E0301 to E0303 or E0400, which accepted RFCs already use, so the RFC cannot merge as written. I would approve if Cost names one removal the checklist would notice and the catalogue gap is fixed in the same change.

The design is implementable from its text. It names every built-in, the copy and borrow rules, the trap kinds and the two new codes, and its test plan covers each new code. It fixes the defects this implementer found in 0029: the untestable trap-oom count, the undefined capacity, and the duplicated trap list. Conditions before merge, which the RFC already states: spec/errors.json must gain E0203 and E0401 and the codes from accepted RFCs (#72), and the roadmap question (open question 3) must be settled. The vote does not waive either condition. The RFC is a retry of rejected 0029 and the 0029 vote record gives no reasons, so the designer should say which part changed in response.

Not ready to accept. (1) The test plan contradicts R17 and R18: R17 says any function that builds an array literal with n >= 1, copies a name, or calls push must declare alloc, and R18 says main follows R17, yet the run tests (arr-literal-len, arr-copy-let, arr-copy-assign, arr-set and others) are described with main and no alloc, so as written they would fail with E0401. (2) The RFC cannot merge while spec/errors.json lacks E0200, E0201, E0202, E0300, E0301, E0303 and E0400, which it uses, and it adds E0203 and E0401 without entries; I checked the file and only E0100 of these codes is present. (3) It is a near-copy of RFC 0029, which was rejected with no recorded reason, and the RFC does not say which design objection it answers. The design itself (copy on bind, borrow on call, alloc in the signature, bump allocator with defined traps) is sound, so a revision that fixes the test plan, lists the catalogue entries, and names the answer to the 0029 objection should be re-proposed.

As an everyday user I need a growable list for text lines and numbers, and this gives one type with get, set, push and len. Traps on a bad index and on an exhausted heap give defined results instead of silent corruption. My vote rests on the assignment summary only: the card does not yet mention arrays, and I did not read the RFC text or confirm any of the built-ins by running them.

I write parsers and data models, and both need a growable array of Int or Byte. The summary adds no token or keyword, keeps one array type, and makes bad index and heap exhaustion defined traps, which fits the no-undefined-behaviour rule. Concerns I accept: binding copies the whole array, and with no free a long-running program only grows its heap. I judged this from the assignment summary only; I did not read the RFC text.

data.body: Cut `text_cat` and `text_slice` from this RFC and leave them for the arrays-buffers item. Those two are the only allocating functions, so cutting them removes TX12, TX13 and open question 3, and the out-of-memory trap with them. That also fixes a contradiction: Motivation says the draft adds no trap kind, but TX13 adds `out-of-memory`. What remains, `text_len`, `text_byte`, and `==`/`!=`, is pure, needs no memory decision, and still meets the `text` item's indexing and comparison words. The Cost section then lists its removals. If the team reads `building` as a hard requirement of the checklist, the author should say so in Motivation and keep `text_cat` as the only allocating function, with TX13 narrowed to it.

Cut Arr<Int> from this RFC until a finding asks for it. The Motivation names two needs: an output byte buffer for the stage 0 encoder, which Arr<Byte> covers, and a growable token list, which neither element type covers because Text is excluded. No cited issue or benchmark asks for Int arrays. Dropping them removes the Int layout in R2, the mixed-element rule in R9, the Int copy and test cases, and the squares example. That is the named removal the Cost section lacks. If the token list still needs storage after that cut, say which element type it uses instead of adding Int.

I would cut the out-of-memory trap in TX13, or else write it into the contract. The Summary says the only way an operation stops the program is memory exhaustion, "named in the Behaviour column and nowhere else", and TX4 says every function returns a value for every input. But the Behaviour column for text_cat and text_slice does not name out-of-memory; only TX13 does, and the Effects column just says "allocates". Either add the trap to those two rows and qualify the "every input" claim, or drop TX13 and oom.test and say that allocation failure is outside this RFC's total-function claim. The second option keeps the RFC free of a trap kind until issue #64 is settled, which is the RFC's own stated aim.

data.rationale: TX4 makes text_cat and text_slice allocate, but no signature shows it, against principle 3 and against RFC 0034 R17. One change would make me approve: require `alloc` on any function whose body calls text_cat or text_slice. The Cost section also says the new errors use E0200 and E0300, which spec/errors.json does not list (it has E0001, E0005, E0006, E0010, E0100 and E0500), so those must be catalogued in the same change.

The Cost section names no removal, though the designer rules require every addition to name one, and the RFC adds a type form, an effect word, six built-ins, two trap kinds and copy rules. Also E0200, E0300, E0301, E0303, E0630 and E0631 are not in spec/errors.json, so the check job would fail. One change would make me approve: name an accepted construct this removes, such as folding the copy rules R19 and R21 into one rule, and catalogue all six codes in the same change.

The RFC's own Motivation says no benchmark finding concerns arrays, and its Cost section names no removal, though the designer rules require one for every addition. It also proposes a new RFC before a compiler is on main, which ROADMAP.md forbids (issue #74 says check still exits 2.) I would approve if Cost names a removed construct and the vote waits until the first merge puts a compiler on main.

The constitution (principle 3) says whether a function can allocate or fail must be visible in its signature, but TX13 adds an out-of-memory trap to text_cat and text_slice that the TX4 table does not show, and the Summary and TX4 still say every call returns a value. Change: add a trap marker to the TX4 effect column and signatures for text_cat and text_slice, reword the Summary and TX4 to match, and cite E0200 rather than E0100 for TX11, since spec/errors.json defines E0100 as a syntax error.

Proposed during M2b, which architecture/ROADMAP.md says must not happen before the first compiler merges; the draft itself asks for withdrawal in that case. On substance: text_cat and text_slice allocate and can trap out-of-memory, but their signatures show no effect, which conflicts with constitution principle 3. TX8 says RFC 0024 is not accepted, but RFC 0024 is accepted. Resubmit after the first merge, with the allocation effect shown in the signature.

Proposed during M2b, which architecture/ROADMAP.md says must not happen before the first compiler merges; the draft itself asks for withdrawal in that case. On substance the design fits principles 2, 3 and 7 and builds on accepted RFCs 0020 and 0024. It is not ready to decide: E0630 and E0631 are not in spec/errors.json, the traps are not in signatures (issue #64 is open), and the copy-on-bind rule (open question 2) has no reviewer position yet. Resubmit after the first merge.

Reject as drafted. (1) Roadmap: architecture/ROADMAP.md, M2b, says no new RFC is proposed until the first compiler merges onto main. This is proposed before that. (2) TX13 adds a trap kind, out-of-memory, but the Cost section says no trap kind is added. (3) TX4 says every function returns a value for every input, but text_cat and text_slice can trap out-of-memory. (4) TX8 says the byte type is not yet accepted, but rfcs/0024-byte-type.md has status accepted, so text_byte's Int return rests on a false premise. (5) text_cat and text_slice allocate, but the signature shows no effect mark, which principle 3 asks for. (6) The oom test depends on a heap limit that RFC 0033 never sets. I checked the expected values of the len, slice, byte and equality tests against TX4 and TX9 and they match. The design is otherwise coherent; a revised draft that fixes items 2 to 5 could be voted on after the first merge.

Reject as drafted. (1) Roadmap: same M2b clause as RFC 0033; no new RFC before the first compiler merges onto main. (2) E0630 and E0631 fall outside every code range in spec/card.md. E0631 is an effect error and belongs in E0400 to E0499. (3) R17 requires an alloc mark for any call that allocates, but RFC 0033's text_cat and text_slice allocate with no mark. If both are accepted, a function can allocate text with no signature mark. The two drafts need one rule. (4) RFC 0033 treats the byte type as not accepted, while this draft builds on accepted RFC 0024. The two drafts disagree on that premise. (5) Test err-eq, `if array(1) == array(1) { }`, names no enclosing function. If that function lacks alloc, R17 also reports E0631 at the first array call, but the test expects only E0200. The run tests call array() and squares() from main, and main's signature is not stated, so each test must state it. (6) get, set and the two new traps sit outside signatures, which principle 3 disfavours. The draft marks this as open, which is fair. The points I checked otherwise agree with RFC 0020 and RFC 0024: the grammar, byte() and int(), and the E0300 and E0303 uses.

As a user writing small text tools, I want Text operations that never trap on a bad index or bounds. The summary says every call returns one defined value, and no ordering keeps the surface small. I judged this from the summary only; the spec card does not yet cover Text operations, so I could not run them.

A growable array with copy-on-bind is easy to reason about for a user, and a defined trap with exit 1 on a bad index is clearer than silent behaviour. I judged this from the summary only; the spec card does not yet mention Arr, array, get, set, push or len, so I could not test the syntax or the trap message.

As a user writing parsers, I need text operations that never stop the program on a bad index or bounds. Total operations with one defined result for every input let me write parsing code without guarding every call. I judged from the assignment summary only. The Behaviour table was not in my assignment, so I did not check each function's result against it.

Int and Byte arrays with array, get, set, push and len cover the data-modelling and parsing work I do. Defined traps with exit status 1 on a bad index or exhausted heap are acceptable. Two points for the author: the summary says no keyword is added, yet 'alloc' is a new effect word; and copying an array on every bind, assign and return may be costly for large arrays. I judged from the summary only.

data.body: Cut `text_len` before adding anything. `text_byte` already returns `-1` for every index outside the text (TX2), so a program finds the length with a loop that stops at the first `-1`: `var i = 0` then `while text_byte(t, i) != -1 { i = i + 1 }`. That removes one signature (TX2), one reserved name (TX5), one card line, and the `len` test, and it shrinks the Cost estimate. The `-1` rule is what makes the loop safe, because byte values are 0 to 255 and `-1` cannot be data. If the team still wants `text_len` for speed, the RFC should name the loop it saves and argue for it on that basis.

Cut TX8, the mixed-type rule for == and !=. It says a Text compared with a non-Text is a type error, which E3 already implies once Text is a distinct type. Restating it ties this RFC to issue #31, adds no test (the test plan says so), and leaves a second place where the diagnostic code must be decided. If E3 does not already reject mixed operands, put that one clause in E3 and reference it from TX6 instead.

1. parse-not-binds (compile-error): `fn main() io { let a = 1; let b = 2; if not a == b { print(1) } }`, with the lines split as in the file. Expected: E0200 on line 4 only. Exit 1. Reading: (not a) == b, so `not` gets an Int operand (E5).
2. parse-neg-mul-binds (run): `let a = 4611686018427387904; let b = 2; print(-a * b)`. Expected stdout `-9223372036854775808`, exit 0. Reading (-a) * b. The other reading, -(a * b), traps overflow.
3. parse-not-and (run): `if not false and false { print(1) } else { print(2) }`. Expected stdout `2`, exit 0. Reading (not false) and false.
4. parse-and-or (run): `if true or true and false { print(1) }` then `if false and false or true { print(2) }`. Expected stdout `1` then `2`, exit 0. The and binds tighter than or.
5. parse-arith-assoc (run): `print(2 + 3 * 4)`, `print(10 - 4 - 3)`, `print(7 / 2 * 2)`. Expected stdout `14`, `3`, `6`, exit 0. Left associative.
6. parse-cmp-paren (run): `if (1 < 2) == (2 < 3) { print(1) }`. Expected stdout `1`, exit 0.
7. parse-cmp-chain-lt (compile-error): `let d = a < b < c` on line 5. Expected E0100 on line 5. Exit 1.
8. parse-cmp-chain-mixed (compile-error): `if a == b >= c { print(1) }` on line 5. Expected E0100 on line 5. Exit 1.
9. parse-literal-max (run): `let m = 9223372036854775807; print(m)`. Expected stdout `9223372036854775807`, exit 0.
10. parse-literal-min-expr (run): `let m = -9223372036854775807 - 1; print(m)`. Expected stdout `-9223372036854775808`, exit 0. The spec's way to write MIN (T1).
11. parse-literal-over (compile-error): `let m = 9223372036854775808` on line 2. Expected E0500 on line 2. Exit 1.
12. parse-literal-neg-min (compile-error): `let m = -9223372036854775808` on line 2. Expected E0500 on line 2. Exit 1. T1 counts the sign.
13. parse-unary-plus (compile-error): `let a = +1` on line 2. Expected E0100 on line 2. Exit 1. E6.

Open point for the architect: case 1 expects one E0200. If the checker reports a second error at the `==` (its left side is ill-typed), the case fails. RFC 0020 does not define error recovery, so please say which is intended.

data.body: Cut TX8 before anything else. It adds a rule for `==` with one Text operand and one operand of another type, but it names no diagnostic code (the code is left to issue #31), and the test plan has no test for it, so it is a rule with no code and no test. If RFC 0020 E3 already requires both operands of `==` to have the same type, then the Text case is covered by that rule and TX8 can go. If E3 does not say that, add the one clause to E3 and drop TX8. This keeps the step to the two built-in signatures plus Text equality, which is the smallest version of this RFC.

Cut TX7 and TX8. RFC 0020 E3 and E4 already say that any operand of the wrong type for `==`, `!=`, `<`, `<=`, `>` or `>=` is E0200. So a `Text` operand under `<` or `>` is already E0200, and a mixed `Text`/`Int` `==` is already E0200 once E3 admits `Text` as its own case. TX8 also names no code, which conflicts with the catalogue check, and neither TX7 nor TX8 has a conformance test, which conflicts with the rule that every construct is tested. Remove both. Replace TX6 with one sentence: `==` and `!=` also take two `Text` operands and compare them byte for byte. The ordering question (#69) then stays with E4, where it belongs.

data.rationale: Adds about 150 core-spec tokens (two built-ins, a Text case of == and !=, two reserved names) and removes only two restated sentences from RFC 0020 T3 and E3, so it does not pay for itself under the rule that every addition needs a removal. To approve, name in Cost a removal from the core spec that covers the net growth; TX7 and TX8 can also name E0200 now, as RFC 0020 E3 and E4 already do, instead of waiting on issue #31.

TX2 gives both built-ins one defined result for every argument (`-1` out of range), and TX3 rules out traps and allocation, so principles 3 and 7 hold without deciding #64. The codes it uses (E0001, E0005, E0100, E0200, E0300) are already in spec/errors.json, and TX8's mixed-type case already falls under E3's E0200 wording.

Small and total: two built-ins that cannot fail, no trap kind, no allocation, and no decision on issue #64 needed. Checked against the repo: the rules it amends (T3, E3, F6) and the codes it uses (E0001, E0005, E0100) match RFC 0020 and spec/errors.json. Non-blocking note: E3 already sends any operand pair without a matching type to E0200, so the mixed-type == case in TX8 does not need to wait for issue #31. The RFC could state E0200 now, with its test.

The test plan contradicts RFC 0020 P1 and P2. P1 says print takes only Int or Text, and print(true) is E0200 (test err-print-bool). So the run tests text/equal.test, which expect print("ab" == "ab") to print true, have no valid expected output as written. Fix: print an Int inside an if, for example if "ab" == "ab" { print(1) }, and then the tests can be derived from the spec. The design itself is sound: the two functions are total and add no trap. Also, TX8 says the mixed-type code is unsettled, but RFC 0020 E3 already gives E0200, so that sentence is out of date. I would change to approve once the equality tests are fixed.

As a user writing small text tools, I need to check the length of a string and read its bytes, and I need to compare two strings with ==. This RFC adds exactly those and nothing else, and both functions are total with a defined result, which fits the no-undefined-behaviour principle. I could not check the details: spec/card.md has no Text section yet, so I cannot confirm the signatures or the == rules from the card.

As a parsing user I need to measure a text and compare two texts, and this RFC gives exactly that with total functions and no new heap values. I could only judge from the summary: the spec card does not mention Text, so I have not checked the exact semantics of text_byte past the summary.

data.body:
Tester cases for subtask 6 (`parse-expr.ts`, RFC 0020 precedence list, G6, T1, E6).

State of the checkout: the lexer, `span.ts`, `diagnostic.ts`, and the E0100 and E0500 entries in `spec/errors.json` are all present, and `compiler/stage0/src/kernel/parse-expr.test.ts` already asserts the six cases the assignment names. I read that file and did not run it. The table below lists those six, plus cases it does not cover. I wrote no code or test files.

How to read the table: offsets are byte offsets from the start of the input, and a span is `start..end`. Exit 0 means the parser returns a tree. Exit 1 means it returns one error record, which is what `glyphc check` exits with (subtask 18).

| # | Input | Expected output | Exit | Why |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 1 | `not a == b` | `(== (not a) b)` | 0 | named; `not` binds tighter than `==` |
| 2 | `-a * b` | `(* (- a) b)` | 0 | named; unary binds tighter than `*` |
| 3 | `a < b < c` | E0100 at 6..7 (second `<`) | 1 | named; G6 |
| 4 | `a == b >= c` | E0100 at 7..9 (`>=`) | 1 | named; G6 |
| 5 | `-9223372036854775808` | E0500 at 1..20 (literal) | 1 | named; T1, after unary `-` |
| 6 | `+1` | E0100 at 0..1 (`+`) | 1 | named; E6 |
| 7 | `a < b >= c` | E0100 at 6..8 (`>=`) | 1 | G6, mixed operators |
| 8 | `a != b != c` | E0100 at 7..9 (second `!=`) | 1 | G6, same operator twice |
| 9 | `a == b == c` | E0100 at 7..9 (second `==`) | 1 | G6 |
| 10 | `(a < b) < c` | `(< (< a b) c)` | 0 | parentheses make a primary, so G6 does not apply |
| 11 | `a < (b < c)` | `(< a (< b c))` | 0 | same, on the right |
| 12 | `a < b and b < c` | `(and (< a b) (< b c))` | 0 | one comparison on each side of `and` |
| 13 | `a or b and c or d` | `(or (or a (and b c)) d)` | 0 | `or` is left-associative; `and` binds tighter |
| 14 | `not a < b` | `(< (not a) b)` | 0 | `not` is level 6, comparison is level 3 |
| 15 | `1 - -1` | `(- 1 (- 1))` | 0 | unary minus as right operand |
| 16 | `a + 1 < b * 2` | `(< (+ a 1) (* b 2))` | 0 | precedence of `+`, `*` against `<` |
| 17 | `- f(1)` | `(- f(1))` | 0 | a call binds tighter than unary |
| 18 | `(a + [NEWLINE] b)` | `(+ a b)` | 0 | `[NEWLINE]` is a real line end inside `( )`, which is never emitted (RFC 0014 rule 14) |
| 19 | `9223372036854775807` | `9223372036854775807` | 0 | largest `Int` is accepted (boundary) |
| 20 | `-9223372036854775807 - 1` | `(- (- 9223372036854775807) 1)` | 0 | the minimum written as T1 says |
| 21 | `- 9223372036854775808` | E0500 at 2..21 (literal) | 1 | a space after unary `-` does not change the literal error |
| 22 | `--9223372036854775808` | E0500 at 2..21 (literal) | 1 | two unary minus signs |
| 23 | `not 9223372036854775808` | E0500 at 4..23 (literal) | 1 | literal after `not` |
| 24 | `-+1` | E0100 at 1..2 (second `+`) | 1 | `+` is not unary anywhere (E6) |

Left out on purpose, because the spec does not say where they are reported: a missing operand at the end of a line or file (`a +`), and a line end after a binary operator outside parentheses (G2). Also left out: leading zeros, where RFC 0014 rule 8 and RFC 0004 disagree (open question 3 in RFC 0020).

No case here is marked as expected to fail. Every expected value above follows from the RFC 0020 text, so a disagreement with the parser is a finding for the implementer.
